fields.title: The Inner Chamber
fields.description: The Inner Chamber leads readers on a profound spiritual journey, stressing the importance of relying on God’s wisdom over human understanding. Through biblical insights, it reveals that true understanding comes from a humble heart guided by the Holy Spirit.

fields.title: The Morning Hour
fields.body_html:
“O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch.” — Psalms 5:3.

“The Lord God has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” — Isaiah 50:4.

From the earliest times, God’s servants have seen the morning as the right time for worshipping God. All Christians still regard it as both a duty and a privilege to give some part of the beginning of the day to seeking fellowship with God. Many Christians, especially in the Student Christian Association, keep what they call the Morning Watch; the Young People’s Society of Christian Endeavor speaks of it as the Quiet Hour; others call it the Still Hour or the Quiet Time.

All of them — whether they have in mind a whole hour, half an hour or a quarter of an hour — join the Psalmist in saying, “O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice.”

Speaking of how vitally important this daily quiet time of prayer and meditation on God’s Word is, Mr. Mott has said: “Next to receiving Christ as Saviour, and claiming the baptism of the Holy Spirit, we know of no act that brings greater good to ourselves or to others than forming a firm resolution to keep the Morning Watch, and to spend the first half-hour of the day alone with God.” At first glance the statement seems too strong. Receiving Christ as Saviour has infinite consequences for eternity. Claiming the Holy Spirit brings about a revolution in the Christian life. Beside them, something as simple as a firm decision to keep the Morning Watch hardly seems important enough to stand next in line.

But think how impossible it is to live our daily lives in Christ as our Saviour from sin, or to keep walking in the leading and power of the Holy Spirit, without close, daily fellowship with God. Then we will soon see the truth of what he says. For the Morning Watch simply means a settled decision that Christ shall have the whole of life, and that the Holy Spirit shall be fully obeyed in everything. The Morning Watch is the key position from which our surrender to Christ and the Holy Spirit can be kept up fully and without a break.

To see this, let us first look at what the aim of the Morning Watch ought to be. The Morning Watch must not be treated as an end in itself.

It is not enough that it gives us a blessed time of prayer and Bible study, and so brings us a measure of refreshment and help. It is meant to be a means to an end. And that end is to make sure of Christ’s presence for the whole day. Personal devotion to a friend or to a pursuit means that the friend or the pursuit always keeps its place in the heart, even when other matters take up our attention. Personal devotion to Jesus means that we let nothing separate us from Him for a single moment.

To abide in Him and in His love, to be kept by Him and by His grace, to do His will and please Him — for someone truly devoted to Him, this simply cannot be an on-and-off affair. “I need Thee every hour”; “Moment by moment I am kept in His love.” These hymns speak the language of life and truth. “In Thy name shall they rejoice all the day”; “I the Lord do keep it; I will water it every moment.” These are words of divine power. The believer cannot stand for a single moment without Christ. Personal devotion to Him refuses to be satisfied with anything less than abiding always in His love and His will. Nothing less is the true, scriptural Christian life. Only when we see this as its first aim can we see how important and how blessed the Morning Watch is, and what it is really for.

The clearer the goal we are pursuing, the better we can fit the means to reach it. Now look at the Morning Watch as the means to this great end: I want to make absolutely sure of Christ’s presence all day long, and to do nothing that could get in its way. I see at once that my success for the day will depend on how clear and how strong the faith is that seeks Him, finds Him and holds on to HIM in the secret place. Meditation, prayer and the Word will all serve this one purpose and help it along: in the morning hour the link between Christ and me for the day must be renewed and firmly fastened. At first it may seem that thinking about the whole day, with all its possible cares, pleasures and temptations, will disturb the rest I have found in my quiet devotion. That may happen, but it will be no loss.

True religion aims to have the character of Christ so formed in us that His temper and disposition show themselves even in our most ordinary actions. The Spirit and the will of Christ are meant to possess us so fully that, in our dealings with others, in our leisure and in our business, acting in line with them becomes second nature to us. All this is possible because Christ Himself, as the Living One, lives in us. Do not be troubled if at first the aim seems too high or too hard, and takes up too much of your time in the hour of private prayer. The time you give to it will be richly repaid. You will come back to prayer and Scripture with fresh purpose and fresh faith.

As the Morning Watch begins to shape the day, the day in turn will shape your first half-hour, and fellowship with Christ will take on new meaning and new power. In particular, it will affect the spirit in which you keep the Morning Watch.

The aim is grand — unbroken fellowship with God in Christ throughout the day. The means of securing it is real — a definite, conscious meeting with Christ, in which we make sure of His presence for the day. As these two take hold of us, we will see that the one essential thing is wholehearted purpose: a settled determination to win the prize, whatever effort or self-denial it may cost. Every student knows, whether in study or on the sports field, how much a strong will and a determined purpose are needed if we are to succeed.

Religion needs — and truly deserves — not less but more intense devotion. Surely, if anything does, the love of Christ calls for the whole heart. It is this settled determination to secure Christ’s presence before everything else that will overcome every temptation to be unfaithful or careless in keeping our promises. It is this will that makes the Morning Watch itself a mighty means of grace, strengthening our character and steeling us to say No to every call to indulge ourselves. It is this will that, the moment we enter the inner chamber and shut the door, enables us to be there with our whole heart, ready at once for oneness with Christ. And it is this determination that, from the Morning Watch onward, will become the keynote of our daily life.

People in the world often say: Great things are possible for anyone who knows what he wants, and wants it with all his heart.

The student who has made personal devotion to Christ his watchword will find the morning hour to be the place where his sense of his holy calling is renewed day by day; where his will is strengthened to live worthy of it; and where his faith is rewarded by the presence of Christ, who is waiting to meet him and take charge of him for the day. We are more than conquerors through Him who loves us. A living Christ is waiting to meet us.

fields.title: The Door Shut — Alone with God
fields.body_html:
“But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you...” Matthew 6: 6.

Man was created for fellowship with God. God made him in His own image and likeness so that he would be fit for this — able to understand and enjoy God, to enter into His will and to delight in His glory. Because God is everywhere present and fills all things, man could have lived in the enjoyment of unbroken fellowship with Him in the middle of whatever work he had to do.

Sin robbed us of this fellowship.

Nothing but this fellowship can satisfy the heart of either man or God. It was this that Christ came to restore: to bring His lost creature back to God, and to bring man back to all he was created for. Oneness with God is the crowning of all blessedness, on earth as in heaven. It comes when the promise so often given becomes a full experience — “I will never leave you nor forsake you” — and when we can say, The Father is always with me. This oneness with God is meant to be ours all day long, whatever our situation and whatever the circumstances around us. But whether we enjoy it depends on how real that oneness is in the inner chamber. Our power to keep up close and joyful fellowship with God all day will depend entirely on how intensely we seek to secure it in the hour of secret prayer. The one essential thing in the Morning Watch or the Quiet Hour is this — fellowship with God. This is what our Lord teaches us is the inner secret of secret prayer: “Shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret” Matthew 6:6.

The first and chief thing is to make sure that there, in secret, you have the Father’s presence and attention. Know that He sees you and hears you. More important than all your requests, however urgent, and more important than all your earnestness and effort to pray rightly, is this one thing: the childlike, living assurance that your Father sees you, that you have now met Him, and that with His eye on you and yours on Him, you are now enjoying real oneness with Him.

Christian, you face a terrible danger in your inner chamber. You are in danger of putting prayer and Bible study in the place of living fellowship with God — that living exchange in which you give Him your love, your heart and your life, and receive from Him His love, His life and His Spirit.

Your needs and the way you express them, together with your desire to pray humbly, earnestly and in faith, can take up so much of your attention that the light of His face and the joy of His love cannot get in.

Your Bible study can interest you so much, and stir up such pleasant religious feelings, that the very Word of God may become a substitute for God Himself. It then becomes the greatest hindrance to fellowship, because it keeps the soul busy instead of leading it to God Himself. And we go out into the day’s work without the power of an abiding fellowship, because in our morning devotions the blessing was never secured. What a difference it would make in many lives if everything in the secret place were made to serve this one thing: I want to walk with God through the day; my morning hour is the time when my Father makes a definite agreement with me, and I with Him, that it shall be so. What strength would come from knowing: God has taken charge of me; He Himself is going with me; I am going to do His will in His strength all day; I am ready for whatever may come! Yes, what nobility would come into life if secret prayer were not just asking for some fresh sense of comfort, light or strength, but giving our life away, for just this one day, into the sure and safe keeping of a mighty and faithful God!

“Pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.” Where secret fellowship with the Father, in spirit and in truth, is kept up, our public life before others will carry the reward.

The Father who sees in secret takes charge and rewards openly. Withdrawing from people to be alone with God is the sure way — the only way — to live among people in the power of God’s blessing.

fields.title: The Open Door — The Open Reward
fields.body_html:
“But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.” Matthew 6: 17-18.

“Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus.” Acts 4:13.

“When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand as he came down from the mountain, Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God. Aaron and all the people of Israel saw Moses, and behold, the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come near him. But Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses talked with them. Afterward, all the people of Israel came near, and he commanded them all that the LORD had spoken with him in Mount Sinai. And when Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face.” Exodus 34: 29-33.

Moving from fellowship with God in the morning hour to mixing with other people is often difficult. If we have met God, we long to keep the sense of His presence and of our surrender to Him. Then we go out to the breakfast table, perhaps in the heart of our own family, and suddenly the atmosphere changes. As the presence of people and of visible things makes itself felt, we begin to lose what we had found. Many young Christians have been puzzled by the question of how to keep their hearts full of something they do not feel free to talk about, or have no opportunity to talk about. Even among religious people it is not always easy — for lack of warmth or courage — to talk freely about the things that would bring the greatest profit and pleasure. Let us try to learn how our dealings with people can become, not a hindrance, but a help in keeping up a life of continual fellowship with God.

The story of Moses with the veil over his face teaches lessons that are full of meaning. Close and continued fellowship with God will in time leave its mark and show itself to others. Moses did not know that his face shone: the light of God shining from us will be unconscious; it will only deepen our sense of being an earthen vessel (1 Corinthians 2:3, 4 and 2 Corinthians 4). The sense of God’s presence in a person may often make others afraid, or at least ill at ease, in his company. When others notice what can be seen in him, the true believer will know how to veil his face, and to prove by humility and love that he is indeed a man with the same nature as those around him.

And yet, through it all, there will also be proof that he is a man of God, who lives in an unseen world and has dealings with it.

What our Lord says about fasting teaches the same lessons.

Make no show of your fasting, so that people do not see that you are fasting. Meet them in the joy and kindness of God’s gentleness, as the Father’s beloved and loving child. Count on God, who has seen you in secret, to reward you openly: to give you grace in your dealings with people, to keep up your communion with Him, and to let them see that His grace and light are on you.

The story of Peter and John confirms the same truth. They had been with Jesus — not only while He was on earth, but as He entered the heavenly places — and they had received His Spirit. They simply acted out what the Spirit of Christ taught them, and even their enemies could tell from their boldness that they had been with Jesus.

The blessing of fellowship with God can easily be lost by losing ourselves too deeply in the company of others. The spirit of the inner chamber must be carried through the whole day in holy watchfulness. We do not know at what hour the enemy may come. We can carry on the Morning Watch through the day by a quiet self-control, not giving free rein to our natural selves.

In religious homes, people have often found it helpful for each person at the breakfast table to repeat a text on some agreed subject; this makes it easy for spiritual conversation to begin. Once the aim of the morning hour has become an abiding sense of God’s presence and of oneness with Him — “Continue in the fear of the LORD all the day” — together with the deepest humility and the most loving fellowship with those around us, then grace will have been sought and found to go on into the day’s duties with our fellowship unbroken. It is a great thing to enter the inner chamber, shut the door and meet the Father in secret. It is a greater thing to open the door again and go out, enjoying that presence which nothing can disturb.

To some people, such a life does not seem necessary; the strain is too great, and one can be a good Christian without it. But for those who want to be people of one thing — who feel that if they are to be true, and to have a mighty influence on the church and the world around them, they must be full of God and of His presence — everything will give way to the one question: how to carry the heavenly treasure in the earthen vessel, with the power of Christ resting on us all day long.

fields.title: Moses and the Word of God
fields.body_html:
On how prayer and the Word belong together in our private devotions, the words of a convert from heathenism have often been quoted: When I pray, I speak to God; when I read the Bible, God speaks to me. There is a verse in the story of Moses that brings out this thought beautifully. We read in Numbers 7: 89, “And when Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony, from between the two cherubim; and it spoke to him.” When he went in to pray for himself or for his people, and to wait for instructions, he found One waiting for him. What a lesson for our Morning Watch!

A prayerful spirit is a spirit God will speak to. A prayerful spirit will be a listening spirit, waiting to hear what God says. In fellowship with God, His presence and the part He plays must be as real to me as my own. We want to ask what is needed for our Scripture reading and our praying to become this kind of true fellowship with God.

First, get into the right place. “Moses went into the Tabernacle to speak with God.”

He separated himself from the people and went where he could be alone with God. He went to the place where God was to be found. Jesus has told us where that place is. He calls us to go into our room, shut the door and pray to our Father who sees in secret.

Anywhere we are truly alone with God can become for us the secret place of His presence. To speak with God, we need to be separated from everything else. We need a heart firmly set on meeting God personally, fully expecting to meet Him and to deal with Him directly. Those who go there to speak to God will hear the voice of the One who speaks to them.

Next, get into the right position. Moses heard the voice of One speaking from above the mercy seat. Bow before the mercy seat. There, the awareness of your unworthiness will not hold you back but will be a real help in trusting God. Bow before the mercy seat, and be sure that the God of mercy will see you and bless you. Then get into the right frame of mind — the listening attitude. Many people are so taken up with what they have to say in their prayers, whether much or little, that they never hear the voice of the One speaking from above the mercy seat, because they neither expect it nor wait for it.

But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.” Let us go into the secret place and set ourselves to pray with a heart that humbly waits to hear God speak; then, in the Word we read, we will indeed hear the voice of the One who speaks to us.

The highest blessing of prayer will come when we stop praying and let God speak.

fields.title: Moses, the Man of Prayer
fields.body_html:
Before Moses came the age of the patriarchs, with its family life and the authority the fathers held. Marking the change, Moses is the first man appointed to be a teacher and leader of men. In him we find wonderful illustrations of the place and power of intercession in the life of God’s servant.

Moses’ prayers. From his first call in Egypt, Moses prayed. He asked God what he was to say to the people (Exodus 3:11-13). He told Him all his weaknesses and begged to be released from his mission (4:1-13). When the people blamed him because their burdens had grown heavier, he went and told God (5:22), and he made all his fears known to Him (6:12). This was his first training. Out of it grew his power in prayer, when time after time Pharaoh asked him to plead with the Lord for him, and deliverance came at Moses’ request (8:8, 9, 12, 28, 29, 30, 31; 9:28-29, 9:33; 10:17-18). Study these passages until you are fully impressed by how real a part prayer played in Moses’ work and in God’s redemption.

At the Red Sea, Moses cried to God together with the people, and the answer came (14:15).

When the people were thirsty in the wilderness, and when Amalek attacked them, it was again prayer that brought deliverance (17:4, 11).

At Sinai, when Israel had made the golden calf, it was prayer that at once turned away the threatened destruction (32:11, 32:14). It was renewed prayer that won their restoration (32:31). It was still more prayer that secured God’s presence to go with them (33:17), and once again it was prayer that brought the revelation of God’s glory (33:19). And when that had been given, it was fresh prayer that received the renewal of the covenant (34:9-10). In Deuteronomy we have a wonderful summary of all this (9:18-20, 19:26). We see how intensely he prayed, and how on one occasion he lay on his face before the Lord for forty days and forty nights (9:25, 10:10).

In Numbers we read of Moses’ prayer quenching the fire of the Lord (11:2) and obtaining the supply of meat (10:2, 11); of prayer healing Miriam (12:13); and of prayer saving the nation when they had refused to go up into the land (14:17-20). Prayer brought down judgment on Korah (16:15), and when God was about to consume the whole congregation, prayer made atonement (46). Prayer brought water out of the rock (20:6), and in answer to prayer the bronze serpent was given (21:7). Through prayer, God’s will was made known in a difficult case (27:5), and Joshua was given as Moses’ successor (16).

Study all this until your whole heart is filled with the thought of the part prayer must play — and may play — in the life of anyone who wants to be God’s servant to his fellow men.

As we study, the parts will come together into a living whole, and Moses will become for us a living model for our prayer life. We will learn what it takes to be an intercessor. The lessons that come to us will be such as these. I see that Moses was a man given up to God — zealous, yes, jealous for God, for His honour and His will.

He was a man, too, wholly given up to his people, ready to sacrifice himself if only they might be saved.

He was a man conscious of a divine calling to act as a mediator — to be the link, the channel of communication and of blessing, between a God in heaven and people on earth. His life was so entirely possessed by this sense of being a mediator that nothing could be simpler or more natural than to expect God to hear.

I see here that God, in answer to the prayers of one man, saves and blesses those He has entrusted to him, and does what He would not do without those prayers. I see how God, in His whole government of the world, has taken prayer into His plan as one of its essential parts.

I see how heaven is full of the life, power and blessing the earth needs, and how the prayer of the earth is the power that brings that blessing down.

Above all, I see how prayer is a measure of the spiritual life, and how its power depends on my relationship to God and on my awareness of being His representative. He entrusts His work to me, and the simpler and more complete my devotion to His interests, the more natural and certain becomes the assurance that He hears me.

Think of the place God had in Moses’ life: the God who had sent him, the God to whom he was wholly devoted, the God who had promised to be with him, and who would always help him whenever and however he prayed.

Now for the practical application: how can we learn to pray like Moses? We cannot obtain this grace by an act of the will. Our first lesson must be a sense of our own helplessness. Then grace will work it in us, slowly and surely, if we give ourselves up to its training. But although the training will be gradual, there is one thing that can be done at once: we can decide here and now to give ourselves to this life and take up the right position. Do it now. Make the decision to live entirely as a channel through which God’s blessing can flow through you to the world. Take the step.

If you need to, take ten minutes for careful thought. Accept God’s appointment, and take up some particular object of intercession. Take time — a week, say — and get a firm hold of the basic truths that Moses’ example teaches. Just as a music teacher insists on practising the scales — only practice makes perfect — set yourself to learn thoroughly, and to put into practice, these necessary first lessons.

fields.title: Moses, the Man of God
fields.body_html:
“This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the people of Israel before his death.” Deuteronomy 33:1. The man of God! How much that name means! A man who comes from God, chosen and sent by Him. A man who walks with God, lives in His fellowship and carries the mark of His presence. A man who lives for God and His will; whose whole being is filled and ruled by the glory of God; who, without even trying, constantly leads people to think of God. A man in whose heart and life God has taken His rightful place as the All in All, and who has only one desire: that God should have that place throughout the world.

Men of God like this are what the world needs; they are what God is looking for, so that He can fill them with Himself and send them into the world to help others know Him. Moses was so marked by this that people naturally spoke of him this way — Moses, the man of God! Every servant of God ought to aim at being such a man: a living witness and proof of what God is to him in heaven, and is to him on earth, and of what He claims to be in all.

In an earlier chapter we spoke of fellowship with God as what man was created for, as the privilege of daily life, and as what should be our first care in the Morning Watch. What we said there mainly concerned our personal need, and the influence a godly, happy life has on others. The name “Moses the man of God” — the thought of a man so closely and so visibly joined to God that people instinctively named this as his chief characteristic — takes us further.

It brings us out into public life. It points to the impression we make on people, and to the power we can have to carry the sign of God’s holy presence with us, so that when people see us or think of us, the name at once comes to mind — THE MAN OF GOD! These are the men that the world and God both need. Why? Because through sin the world has fallen away from God. Because in Christ the world has been redeemed for God. And because God has no way of showing people what they ought to be — of waking them, calling them and helping them — except through men of God in whom His life, His Spirit and His power are at work.

Man was created for God, so that God might live, dwell, work and show His glory in him and through him. God was to be his all in all. God’s indwelling was meant to be as natural and delightful as it is true, wonderful and beyond understanding. When Christ’s redemption was completed by God the Holy Spirit coming down into human hearts, this indwelling was restored, and God took possession of His home again.

This is where a man gives himself up wholly to the presence of the Holy Spirit — not only as a power working in him, but as God dwelling in him (John 14:16, 14:20, 14:23; 1 John 4). Then he may become, in the deepest sense of the word, A MAN OF GOD! Paul tells us that it is through the power of Holy Scripture that “the man of God is complete.”

“All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.” This brings us back again to the Morning Watch as the chief time for personal Bible study. As we yield our heart and life to the Word, we let God, through its teaching, its reproof, its correction and its instruction, search and shape our whole life. In this way we come under the direct working of God and into full fellowship with Him — and so the man of God becomes complete, equipped for every good work.

Oh, for grace to be truly a man of God! A man who knows and proves these three things: God is all; God claims all; God works all. A man who has seen the place God has in His universe and in human beings — He is the All in All! A man who has understood that God asks for all and must have all, and who lives only to give God what is due to Him, and His glory! A man who has discovered the great secret that God works all, and who seeks, like the Son of God, to live in that constant, blessed dependence in which the Father in Him speaks the words and does the work.

Brother, seek to be a man of God! Let God be everything to you in the Morning Watch. Let God be everything to you during the day. And let your life be devoted to one thing — bringing people to God and God to people — so that God may have His rightful place in His Church and in the world.

“If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven.” That was Elijah’s answer when the captain called him to come down. The true God is the God who answers by fire, and the true man of God is the one who knows how to call down the fire, because he has power with the God of heaven. Whether the fire is the fire of judgment or of the Holy Spirit, the work of the man of God is to bring fire down to earth. What the world needs is the man of God who knows God’s power and his own power with God.

Believe that it is in the daily habit of secret prayer that we learn to know our God, His fire and our power with Him. Oh, to know what it is to be a man of God, and all that it means!

In Elijah, as in Moses, we see that it simply means separation from every other interest — complete identification with the honour of God — no longer a man of the world, but a man of God. We secretly feel that all this brings more strain and sacrifice, difficulty and danger, than we are ready for. That is only true as long as we have not seen how absolute God’s claim is, how indescribably blessed it is to yield to it, and how certainly God Himself will work it in us.

Now turn back and look at Moses, the man of prayer, Moses the man of the world, and see how out of these grew Moses, the man of God. See the same in the life of Elijah: the harmony between our hearing God’s Word and His hearing ours, and the way it becomes divinely possible to be, and to live as, A MAN OF GOD. And then study how it applies to you.

fields.title: The Power of God's Word
fields.body_html:
“And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.” — 1 Thessalonians 2: 13.

The value of a person’s words depends on how well I know the one who speaks. What a difference it makes when someone promises me, I will give you half of all I have — whether the speaker is a poor man who owns a shilling, or a millionaire offering to share his fortune with me. One of the first requirements for fruitful Bible study is to know God as the Almighty One, and to know the power of His Word. The power of God’s Word is infinite. “By the word of the Lord were the heavens made. He spoke and it was done; He commanded and it stood fast” Psalms 33:9. In the Word of God, His almighty power is at work: it has creative power, and calls into being the very thing it speaks of.

The word of the living God is a living word that gives life. It can not only call things into being; it can even bring back to life what is dead.

Its life-giving power can raise dead bodies and give eternal life to dead souls. All spiritual life comes through it, for we are born again of incorruptible seed, by the word of God, which lives and abides for ever. Here lies one of the deepest secrets of the blessing of God’s Word, though it is hidden from many: faith in its creative and life-giving energy. The Word will work in me the very disposition or grace that it commands or promises. “It works effectually in them that believe.” Nothing can resist its power when it is received into the heart through the Holy Spirit. “It works effectually in them that believe.” “The voice of the Lord is in power.”

Everything depends on learning the art of receiving that Word into the heart. And in learning this art, the first step is faith — faith in its life, its almighty power and its creative power. It is by His word — “as it is written, ‘I have made you the father of many nations’—in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” Romans 4:17. This is true of all God’s mighty deeds, from creation right through to the resurrection of the dead, and it is just as true of every word spoken to us in His holy Book. Two things keep us from believing this as we should.

The first is the terrible experience, all around us and perhaps in ourselves as well, of the Word being made of no effect by human wisdom, unbelief or worldliness. The second is that we neglect what Scripture teaches — that the Word is a seed.

Seeds are small; seeds may lie dormant for a long time; seeds have to be hidden; and when they sprout, they grow slowly. Because the working of God’s Word is hidden and unnoticed, slow and apparently weak, we do not believe in its almighty power. Let us make this one of our first lessons: the Word I study is the power of God for salvation; it will work in me all I need, and all the Father asks.

What a prospect this faith would open up for our spiritual life! We would see all the treasures and blessings of God’s grace within our reach. The Word has power to light up our darkness: it will bring into our hearts the light of God, the sense of His love and the knowledge of His will. fields.title: The Seed Is the Word
fields.body_html:
I think it can be said with confidence that nothing in all of nature illustrates what the Word of God is as truly, or as richly, as the seed does. To gain full spiritual insight into this is a wonderful means of grace. The points of likeness are easy to list. There is the seed’s apparent insignificance — a tiny thing compared with the tree that springs from it. There is life, shut up and dormant inside a husk. There is the need for suitable soil, without which there can be no growth. There is slow growth, taking a long time and calling for the farmer’s long patience. And there is the fruit, in which the seed reproduces and multiplies itself. In all these ways the seed teaches us the most precious lessons about how we use God’s Word.

First there is the lesson of faith. Faith does not look at appearances.

As far as we can tell, it seems most unlikely that a word of God should give life in the soul, work in us the very grace it speaks of, transform our whole character and fill us with strength. And yet that is how it is. Once we have learned to believe that the Word can effectively bring about the very truth it expresses, we have found one of the chief secrets of Bible study. We will then receive each word as the promise, and the power, of God at work.

Then there is the lesson of labour. The seed has to be gathered, kept and put into prepared soil. In the same way, the mind has to gather from Scripture the words that meet our need, understand them and pass them on to the heart — the only soil in which this heavenly seed can grow. We cannot give life or growth. Nor do we need to: the life is already there. But what we can do is hide the Word in our heart and keep it there, waiting for the sunshine that comes from above.

The seed also teaches the lesson of patience. In most cases the Word does not take effect on the heart immediately. It needs time to take root and grow up: Christ’s words must abide in us. We must not only add to our store of Bible knowledge day by day — that is only like gathering grain into a barn — but also watch over the particular words of command or promise we have taken to ourselves, and give them room in our heart to spread both root and branches. We need to know what seed we have planted, and to cultivate a watchful, patient expectation. In due time we shall reap, if we faint not (Galatians 6:9).

Last comes the lesson of fruitfulness. However insignificant that little seed of a word of God may look, however weak its life may seem, however deeply hidden the very thought of what it speaks of may be, and however much the slowness of its growth may try our patience — be sure the fruit will come. The very truth, life and power of God that the word held in thought will grow and ripen in you. And just as a seed bears fruit that contains the same seed for new growth, so the Word will not only bring you the fruit it promised; that fruit will each time become a seed you carry to others, to give them life and blessing.

It is not only the Word: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed” Matthew 13:31. All the grace of the kingdom comes in no other way than as a hidden seed in the heart of the born-again believer. Christ is a seed. The Holy Spirit is a seed. The love of God poured out in the heart is a seed. The exceeding greatness of the power that works in us is a seed. The hidden life is there in the heart, but its power is not felt at once, or always. The divine glory is there, but often without form or beauty — to be known only by faith, to be counted on and acted on even when it is not felt, and to be waited for as it springs up and grows.

As this central truth is firmly grasped each time, and held as the law of all heavenly life on earth, the study of God’s Word becomes an act of faith, of surrender and of dependence on the living God. I believe humbly, almost tremblingly, in the divine seed that is in the Word, and in the power of God’s Spirit to make it true in my life and experience. I yield my heart, hungrily and wholly, to receive this divine seed. And I wait on God in complete dependence and confidence to give the increase, with power beyond all we can ask or think.

fields.title: Doing and Knowing
fields.body_html:
“But Jesus said, ‘Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!’” Luke 11:28.

“If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.” John 7: 17.

Some time ago I received a letter from someone who was clearly an earnest Christian, asking me for a few hints to help him in Bible study. My first thought was to reply that there are so many addresses and booklets on the subject that he would find everything I could say already said better. After a while, though, certain experiences in my own immediate circle made me feel how much teaching was needed on this all-important subject, and I found there were points that seemed to deserve special emphasis. I take up my pen with the earnest prayer and hope that what I write may come from God, the fountain of light and life, to help His young children see how they may draw from His precious Word all the divine teaching and nourishment, and all the abundant joy and strength, that He has stored up for them.

I imagine myself speaking to a young Christian who has said to me: “Help me to study my Bible. Give me some rules to guide me in how to begin and how to go on, so that I may know my Bible well.” The very first thing I have to say to him, the thing that comes before everything else, is this: in your Bible study, everything will depend on the spirit in which you come to it — on the object or end you set before yourself. In worldly matters, a person is ruled and driven on by the end or aim he sets before himself. It is no different with the Bible. If your aim is simply to know the Bible well, you will be disappointed. If you think a thorough knowledge of the Bible is bound to be a blessing, you are mistaken.

To some it is a curse. To others it is powerless; it makes them neither holy nor happy. To some it is a burden; it weighs them down instead of bringing them life or lifting them up. What, then, should be the aim or end, the true attitude, of the Bible student? God’s Word is food, bread from heaven; the first need for Bible study is: — A GREAT HUNGER AFTER RIGHTEOUSNESS, a great desire to do all God’s will. The Bible is light: the first condition for enjoying it is a heart that longs to walk in God’s ways. Is this not what the texts I have placed above teach us?

“Blessed are they that hear the word of God and keep it.” There is no blessing in hearing or knowing God’s Word apart from keeping it. The Word is nothing if it is not kept, obeyed and done. “If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know.” John 7:17. According to this saying of our Lord, all true knowledge of God’s Word depends first on the will to do it.

Is this not the very lesson we are pressing home? God will refuse to unlock the real meaning and blessing of His Word to anyone except those whose will is definitely set on doing it. I must read my Bible with one purpose: “Whatsoever He says unto you, do it.”

Why this should be so is easy to see when we think about what words are for. They stand between the will and the deed. A man decides to do something for you; before he does it, he expresses his thought or purpose in words; then he fulfils the words by doing what he promised. It is the same with God. His words take their value from what He does. In creation, His word came with power: He spoke and it was done. In grace, He does what He says. David prays (2 Samuel 7:25), “Do as you have spoken.” Solomon says at the dedication of the temple: “who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth”; “who has performed His word that He spoke”; “who has kept that which you promised”; “who spoke it with your mouth, and has fulfilled with your hand”; “let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken” (2 Chronicles 6: 4, 10, 15, 16, 17). Through the prophets God says, “I the Lord have spoken it; I will do it.” And they say, “What you have spoken, is done.”

The truth and worth of what God promises lie in this: that He does it. His word of promise is meant to be done. This is just as true of His word of command — of the things He means us to do. If we do not do them — if we try to know them, admire their beauty and praise their wisdom, but do not do them — we deceive ourselves. They are meant to be done; only as we do them can their real meaning and blessing be opened up to us.

Only as we do them can we really grow in the divine life. “Walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God.” Only when we come to God’s words with the same purpose God had in giving them — that they should be done — can we have any hope of blessing.

Is this not what we see all around us in the pursuit of knowledge, or in any trade? The apprentice or pupil is expected to put the lessons he receives into practice; only then is he ready for further teaching. It is the same in the Christian life. Bible study remains merely theoretical, a pleasant exercise of the mind and imagination, worth little or nothing for a life of true holiness or Christlikeness, until the student is ready never to open or close his Bible without making God’s purpose his very own, and listening when He says: “Do all that I speak.” This was the mark of the saints of old. “So Abram went, as the LORD had told him.” “This Moses did; according to all that the LORD commanded him, so he did.” This is the description of the man who was faithful as a servant in all God’s house. And of David we read: “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man after my own heart. He will do everything I want him to do.”

In Psalm 119 we hear him speaking with God about His Word and praying for divine light and teaching, but always with a vow of obedience, or some other expression of love and delight, alongside. Even for God’s own Son, doing God’s will is the one secret of entering into the favour and the mind of God.

I have just been reading Mr. Moody’s new book, “Pleasure and Profit in Bible Study.” I have no doubt that many will make use of the suggestions it contains. They will think, rightly, that what helped a man like Moody can help them too. And yet they may be disappointed. They are bound to be, unless they bring to the Bible what Mr. Moody brought: an honest desire to do whatever he saw God wanted him to do. Young Christian, I urge you by the mercies of God: when you ask God to lead you into the treasures of His Word, into the palace where Christ dwells, do it as one who presents himself a living sacrifice, ready to do whatever God says.

Do not think this is something that goes without saying. It is more important than you know. It is missing from Bible study more often than you think. Seek it with deep humility. The first requirement for enjoying your food is hunger. The first requirement for Bible study is a simple, determined longing to find out what God wants you to do, and a dead-earnest resolve to do it. “If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.” To such a person the Word of God will be opened up.

fields.title: The Blessings of the Doer
fields.body_html:
“But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like. But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.” James 1: 22-25. What a terrible delusion it is to be content with hearing the Word, even to delight in hearing it, and yet not do it! And how terribly common it is — the sight of multitudes of Christians who listen to the Word of God very regularly and earnestly, and yet do not do it. If their own servant behaved like that, hearing but not doing, what would they think of him? And yet the delusion is so complete that they never realise they are not living good Christian lives. What can it be that deceives us? There is more than one thing. One is that people mistake the pleasure they get from hearing for religion and worship. The mind delights in having the truth set clearly before it; the imagination is pleased by the pictures it paints; the feelings are stirred by its application.

To an active mind, knowledge gives pleasure. Someone may study a branch of science — electricity, say — for the enjoyment the knowledge gives him, without the slightest intention of putting it to practical use. In the same way, people go to church and enjoy the preaching, and yet do not do what God asks. Unconverted and converted alike are content to go on doing wrong and confessing it, and then still doing the things they ought not to do. Another cause of this delusion is a terrible distortion of the doctrine of our inability to do good. People believe so little in the grace of Christ to enable us to obey, to keep us from sinning and to make us truly holy, that in practice they think sinning is laid on them as a necessity. God cannot expect exact obedience from them, they reason, because He knows they cannot give it. This error cuts away the very root of any determined purpose to do all that God has said. It closes the heart to any earnest desire to believe in and experience all that God’s grace can do in us, and it keeps people self-satisfied in the middle of sin. Hearing and not doing — what terrible self-deception!

There is a third reason for it, which applies especially to private Bible reading. The hearing or reading is regarded as a duty, and carrying out that duty is thought of as a religious service. We have spent our five or ten minutes reading in the morning; we have read thoughtfully and attentively; we have tried to take in what we read. A duty faithfully done eases the conscience and gives a sense of satisfaction.

And there is hardly any understanding of how worthless — and more than that, how hardening — a duty performed or knowledge acquired can be, unless we go out with our whole heart set on literally doing and being what God’s Word says He wants us to be, and can make us. What a terrible delusion! “But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.” James 1:22.

It is in the secret place, in the Morning Watch, that this delusion must be fought and overcome. We may find that this disrupts our regular Bible reading and puts us behind in our portions. It does not need to. But it is far better that it should than that this point should stay doubtful and unsettled. Everything depends on it. Our Lord Jesus said: “If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God.” Only the heart that delights in God’s law and has firmly set its will on doing it can receive the divine light that knows, spiritually, the teaching of Christ in its divine origin and power. Without this will to do, our knowledge will be of no profit: it is mere head knowledge.

In life, in science and art, and in business, the only way of truly knowing is doing. What a person cannot do, he does not thoroughly know. The only way to know God and taste His blessedness is by doing His will. That proves whether the God I confess is a God of my own feelings and imagination, or the true and living God who rules and works all things. Only in doing His will do I prove that I love it and accept it, and make myself one with it. Besides that, there is no possible way under heaven of being united to God except by being united to His will in doing it.

It is in the quietness of the inner chamber — in the spirit in which I do my private Bible reading, and in the determination with which I seek to have this point absolutely and finally settled, I am going to do whatever God says — that the dreadful self-deception of hearing and not doing must be overcome. Suppose it is the Sermon on the Mount. I begin with the first Beatitude: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” I ask: What does this mean? Am I obeying this command? Am I at least thoroughly in earnest in seeking day by day to keep this attitude?

As I feel how far my proud, self-confident nature is from it, am I willing to wait, to plead with Christ, and to believe that He can work it in me? Am I going to do this — to be poor in spirit? Or will I once again be a hearer and not a doer? And so I can go through the Beatitudes and through the whole sermon — its teaching on meekness and mercy, on love and righteousness, on doing everything as to the Father and trusting Him in everything, on doing His will and Christ’s words — and ask: Do I know what this means? fields.title: Keeping Christ's Commandments
fields.body_html:
“If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”— John 13: 17.

The blessedness and blessing of God’s Word can only be known by doing it. The subject is so supremely important in the Christian life, and therefore in our Bible study, that I must ask you to come back to it once more. This time let us take just one expression — keeping the word, or keeping the commandments. Let us look at it first in the farewell discourse. You may know the passages well, but it will be useful to look at them together.

“If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper” (John 14:15, 16).

“Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” (vs.21) “Jesus answered him, ‘If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.’” (vs.23) “If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.” (15:7) “If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.” (15:10) “You are my friends if you do what I command you.” (15:14).

Study and compare these passages until the words sink into your heart and produce the deep conviction that keeping Christ’s commandments is the essential condition of all true spiritual blessing. For the coming of God the Holy Spirit and His actual indwelling; for enjoying the Father’s love; for Christ revealing Himself inwardly; for the Father and the Son making their home in the heart; for power in prayer; for abiding in Christ’s love and enjoying His friendship — keeping the commandments is the one requirement.

And if we are to claim and enjoy these blessings in faith day by day, a childlike awareness that we do keep them is essential too. Just as essential for fruitful Bible study is the quiet assurance that dares to expect divine light and strength with every word of God, because He knows we are ready to obey to the very utmost.

The will of God, delighted in and done, is our only way to the Father’s heart, and His only way to ours.

Keep the commandments: this is the way to every blessing. See how strikingly all this is confirmed by what we find in John’s first letter.

“And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments. Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected.” (1 John 2:3-5). The only proof of a true, living, saving knowledge of God — the only proof that we are not deceiving ourselves in our religion, and that God’s love is not imagined but truly possessed — is keeping His word.

“If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God; and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him. Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God” (3:21, 22, and 24). Keeping the commandments is the secret of confidence before God and of true, intimate fellowship with Him.

“For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world.” (v.3, 4).

Our profession of love is worthless unless it is proved true by keeping His commandments in the power of a life born of God. Knowing God, having the love of God perfected in us, having boldness with God, abiding in Him, being born of Him and loving Him — all of it depends on one thing: KEEPING THE COMMANDMENTS.

Only as we realise how much weight Christ and Scripture give to this truth will we learn to give it the same weight in our own lives. It will become one of the keys to true Bible study for us. The person who reads his Bible with a longing and determined purpose to search out and obey every commandment of God and of Christ is on the right track to receive all the blessing the Word was ever meant to bring. He will learn two things in particular: how much he needs to wait for the teaching of the Holy Spirit to lead him into all God’s will; and what a blessing there is in carrying out daily duties, not only because they are right or because he enjoys them, but because they are the will of God. He will find that the whole of daily life is lifted up when he says, as Christ did: “This charge I have received from my Father.” The Word will become the light and guide by which all his steps are directed.

His life will become the training school in which the sanctifying power and the encouragement of the Word are proved. And so keeping the commandments will be the key to every spiritual blessing.

Make a determined effort to grasp what this life of full obedience means. Take some of Christ’s clearest commands — Love one another: just as I have loved you; you ought to wash each other’s feet; you also should do just as I have done to you — and accept a Christlike love and humility as the law of the supernatural life you are to live. Far from letting a sense of failure or helplessness drive you to despair, or make you settle for what you think is attainable, let it only encourage you to put your hope more fully in Him who, by His Spirit, will work in you both to will and to do.

Once again, our one aim must be perfect harmony between conscience and conduct. Every conviction must be carried out in action. Christ’s commands were meant to be obeyed. If they are not, the accumulation of Scripture knowledge only darkens and hardens us. It produces a satisfaction in the pleasure of gaining knowledge that makes us unfit for the Spirit’s teaching.

I pray that you will not grow tired of my repeating this blessed, solemn message so often. It is in your inner chamber that the question must be settled whether you will keep the commandments of Christ throughout the day. And it is there, too, that it will be settled whether in your future life you will bear the character of someone wholly given up to knowing and doing the will of God.

fields.title: Life and Knowledge
fields.body_html:
“And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” — Genesis 2: 9.

There are two ways of knowing things. One is in the mind, by notion or concept: I know about a thing. The other is in life: I know it by inward experience. A clever blind man can learn all that science teaches about light by having books read to him. A child, or someone from a primitive tribe, who has never thought about what light is, still knows it far better than the blind scholar. The scholar knows all about it by thinking; the child knows it in reality, by seeing and enjoying it.

It is the same in religion. The mind can form thoughts about God from the Bible and know all the doctrines of salvation, while the inner life does not know the power of God to save. That is why we read, “Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.” A person may be able to put beautiful thoughts about love into words; but unless he loves, he does not know God. Only love can know God. The knowledge of God is eternal life.

God’s Word is the word of life. Out of the heart flow the springs of life. The life may be strong even where the mind’s knowledge is weak. And knowledge may be pursued with the greatest diligence and bring great delight, while the life is untouched by it.

An illustration may make this clear. Suppose we could give an apple tree understanding, with eyes to see and hands to work. This might let the apple tree do for itself what the gardener does now — gather manure or bring water. But the inner life of the apple tree would still be the same, entirely different from the understanding that had been added to it. In the same way, the inner divine life in a person is something quite different from the intellect with which he knows about it. The intellect is indeed very necessary, to present to the heart the Word of God, which the Holy Spirit can bring to life. And yet it is completely powerless either to give the true life or to awaken it. It is only a servant carrying the food: it is the heart that must eat, be nourished and live.

The two trees in Paradise are God’s revelation of this same truth. If Adam had eaten from the tree of life, he would have received and known all the good God had for him, as a living power and an experience. He would have known evil only by being entirely free from it. But Eve was led astray by the desire for knowledge — “the fruit was to be desired to make one wise” — and humanity gained a knowledge of good without possessing it, a knowledge of it only through the evil that was its opposite. Ever since that day, man has looked for his religion more in knowledge than in life.

Only life — the experience and possession of God and His goodness — gives true knowledge. The knowledge of the intellect cannot give life. “And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.” 1 Corinthians 13:2. It is in our daily Bible reading that this danger confronts us, and it is there that it must be faced and overcome. We need the intellect to hear and understand God’s Word in its human meaning. But we need to know that holding the truth in the intellect can do us no good unless the Holy Spirit makes it life and truth in the heart. We need to yield our hearts and wait on God, in quiet submission and faith, for Him to work in us by that Spirit. As this becomes a holy habit, we will learn the art of intellect and heart working in perfect harmony, so that every movement of the mind is always matched by a movement of the heart, waiting on and listening for the teaching of the Spirit.

fields.title: The Heart and the Understanding
fields.body_html:
“Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.” Proverbs 3:5. The chief purpose of the book of Proverbs is to teach knowledge and discretion, and to guide us in the path of wisdom and understanding. To understand righteousness, to understand the fear of the Lord, to find good understanding — this is what Proverbs offers to guide us into. But as we pursue this, it warns us to distinguish between trusting our own understanding and intellect, and seeking spiritual understanding — the understanding God gives, an understanding heart: “and lean not to your own understanding.”

In all our seeking after knowledge and wisdom, in all our planning of life or study of the Word, we have these two powers. There is the understanding, or intellect, which knows things from the outside, by their nature and by the concepts we form of them. And there is the heart, which knows them by experience as it takes them up into the will and the affections.

I am deeply convinced that one of the chief reasons why so much Bible teaching and Bible knowledge bears so little fruit — one of the chief causes of the lack of holiness, devotion and power in the Church — is found here: trusting our own understanding in religion. I beg my readers to give me a patient hearing on this.

Many people argue: But surely God gave us our intellect, and without it we cannot possibly know God’s Word. Very true; but listen. Through the Fall, our whole human nature was thrown into disorder. The will became enslaved, the affections were twisted, and the understanding was darkened. Everyone admits that the Fall ruined the first two, but in practice they deny that it ruined the third. They admit that even the believer does not have the power of a holy will in himself, and needs the daily renewing grace of Jesus Christ.

They admit that he does not have the power of holy affection — of loving God and his neighbour — except as it is worked in him continually by the Holy Spirit. But they do not notice that the intellect is just as spiritually ruined and powerless, and unable to grasp spiritual truth.

It was above all the desire for knowledge — in a way and at a time that God had forbidden — that led Eve astray as the outcome of the temptation. To think that we can take the knowledge of God’s truth for ourselves out of His Word, just as we please, is still our greatest danger.

We need a deep conviction of how powerless our understanding is to really know the truth, and of the terrible danger of self-confidence and self-deception in trying, if we are to see our need of the word, “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.” Proverbs 3:5. It is with the heart that man believes. It is with all our heart that we are to seek, serve and love God. It is only with the heart that we can know God, or worship God in spirit and in truth. So it is in the heart that the divine Word does its work. It is into our heart that God has sent the Spirit of His Son. It is the heart — the inner life of desire and love, of will and surrender — that the Holy Spirit guides into all the truth.

In Bible study, “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and lean not to your own understanding.” Do not trust your own understanding — distrust it completely. It can only give you thoughts and ideas of divine things, without the reality. It will deceive you into thinking that the truth, once received into the mind, is sure somehow to enter the heart. And so it will blind you to the terrible fact that everyone can see: people read God’s Word every day and love to hear it every Sunday, and yet it does not make them humble, or holy, or heavenly-minded.

Instead of trusting the understanding, come to the Bible with the heart.

Instead of trusting the understanding, trust in the Lord with all your heart. When you enter your secret place, let the main thing be, not the understanding, but the whole heart set on the living God as its Teacher. Then you will find good understanding. God will give you an understanding heart, a spiritual understanding.

You may ask me, as I have often been asked, “But what am I to do? How am I to study my Bible? I see no way to do it except by using my understanding.” Quite right. But do not use it for what it cannot do. Remember two things. First, it can only give you a picture or a thought of spiritual things. As soon as it has done that, go with your heart to the Lord, for Him to make His Word life and truth in you. Second, remember that pride of intellect — the danger of leaning on your own understanding — never goes away, and that nothing can save you from it, not even the most determined purpose, except the heart’s continual dependence on the Holy Spirit’s teaching. Only by bringing the Word to life in the heart — in the disposition and the affections — can the Holy Spirit guide the intellect. “He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way.” Psalm 25:9. “The fear of the Lord” — a disposition — “is the beginning of wisdom.” Proverbs 9:10. With every thought from the Word that the understanding grasps, bow before God in dependence and trust. Believe with your whole heart that God can and will make it true. Ask the Holy Spirit to make it work effectively in your heart. In this way the Word becomes the strength of our life.

Keep on with this, and the time will come when the Holy Spirit, living in your heart and life, will keep the understanding under His control and let His holy light shine through it.

But as we pursue this, it warns us to distinguish between trusting our own understanding and intellect, and seeking spiritual understanding — the understanding God gives, an understanding heart: “and lean not to your own understanding.” In all our seeking after knowledge and wisdom, in all our planning of life or study of the Word, we have these two powers. There is the understanding, or intellect, which knows things from the outside, by their nature and by the concepts we form of them. And there is the heart, which knows them by experience as it takes them up into the will and the affections. I am deeply convinced that one of the chief reasons why so much Bible teaching and Bible knowledge bears so little fruit — one of the chief causes of the lack of holiness, devotion and power in the Church — is found here: trusting our own understanding in religion. I beg my readers to give me a patient hearing on this. Many people argue: But surely God gave us our intellect, and without it we cannot possibly know God’s Word. Very true; but listen. Through the Fall, our whole human nature was thrown into disorder. The will became enslaved, the affections were twisted, and the understanding was darkened. Everyone admits that the Fall ruined the first two, but in practice they deny that it ruined the third. They admit that even the believer does not have the power of a holy will in himself, and needs the daily renewing grace of Jesus Christ. They admit that he does not have the power of holy affection — of loving God and his neighbour — except as it is worked in him continually by the Holy Spirit. But they do not notice that the intellect is just as spiritually ruined and powerless, and unable to grasp spiritual truth. It was above all the desire for knowledge — in a way and at a time that God had forbidden — that led Eve astray as the outcome of the temptation. To think that we can take the knowledge of God’s truth for ourselves out of His Word, just as we please, is still our greatest danger. We need a deep conviction of how powerless our understanding is to really know the truth, and of the terrible danger of self-confidence and self-deception in trying, if we are to see our need of the word, “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.” Proverbs 3:5. It is with the heart that man believes. It is with all our heart that we are to seek, serve and love God. It is only with the heart that we can know God, or worship God in spirit and in truth. So it is in the heart that the divine Word does its work. It is into our heart that God has sent the Spirit of His Son. It is the heart — the inner life of desire and love, of will and surrender — that the Holy Spirit guides into all the truth. In Bible study, “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and lean not to your own understanding.” Do not trust your own understanding — distrust it completely. It can only give you thoughts and ideas of divine things, without the reality. It will deceive you into thinking that the truth, once received into the mind, is sure somehow to enter the heart. And so it will blind you to the terrible fact that everyone can see: people read God’s Word every day and love to hear it every Sunday, and yet it does not make them humble, or holy, or heavenly-minded. Instead of trusting the understanding, come to the Bible with the heart. Instead of trusting the understanding, trust in the Lord with all your heart. When you enter your secret place, let the main thing be, not the understanding, but the whole heart set on the living God as its Teacher. Then you will find good understanding. God will give you an understanding heart, a spiritual understanding. You may ask me, as I have often been asked, “But what am I to do? How am I to study my Bible? I see no way to do it except by using my understanding.” Quite right. But do not use it for what it cannot do. Remember two things. First, it can only give you a picture or a thought of spiritual things. As soon as it has done that, go with your heart to the Lord, for Him to make His Word life and truth in you. Second, remember that pride of intellect — the danger of leaning on your own understanding — never goes away, and that nothing can save you from it, not even the most determined purpose, except the heart’s continual dependence on the Holy Spirit’s teaching. Only by bringing the Word to life in the heart — in the disposition and the affections — can the Holy Spirit guide the intellect. “He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way.” Psalm 25:9. “The fear of the Lord” — a disposition — “is the beginning of wisdom.” Proverbs 9:10. With every thought from the Word that the understanding grasps, bow before God in dependence and trust. Believe with your whole heart that God can and will make it true. Ask the Holy Spirit to make it work effectively in your heart. In this way the Word becomes the strength of our life. Keep on with this, and the time will come when the Holy Spirit, living in your heart and life, will keep the understanding under His control and let His holy light shine through it.

fields.title: God's Thoughts and Our Thoughts
fields.body_html:
“For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts.” Isaiah 55:9. Even on earth, the words of a wise man often mean something different from what a listener understands by them. How natural, then, that the words of God, as He understands them, should mean something infinitely higher than we grasp at first.

We very much need to remember this. Doing so will keep drawing us away from resting content with our knowledge and our thoughts of the Word, and lead us to wonder and to wait for its full blessing as God intended it. It will give our prayer for the Holy Spirit’s teaching a new sharpness and urgency — that He would show us even what has not yet entered our hearts to imagine. It will give us confidence in the hope that there is for us, even in this life, a fulfilment beyond our highest thoughts.

So God’s Word has two meanings. One is the meaning it has in the mind of God, which makes the human words truly carry all the glory of divine wisdom, power and love. The other is our own weak, partial, imperfect grasp of it. Even after grace and experience have made such words as the love of God, the grace of God and the power of God — or any of the many promises connected with them — very true and real to us, there is still an infinite fullness in the Word that we have not yet known. How strikingly this is put in our text from Isaiah!

“As the heavens are higher than the earth.” Our belief in this fact is so simple and clear that no one would dream of trying to reach the sun or the stars with his little arm. Climbing the highest mountain would not help. We believe it with our whole heart. And now God says, In just the same way, “my thoughts are higher than your thoughts.” Even when the Word has expressed God’s thoughts, and our thoughts have tried to take them in, they still remain as high above our thoughts as the heavens are above the earth. All the infinite things of God and of the eternal world live in the Word as the seed of eternal life. And just as the full-grown oak is so mysteriously greater than the acorn it sprang from, so God’s words are only seeds from which God’s mighty wonders of grace and power can grow.

Faith in this word should teach us two lessons: one of ignorance, the other of expectation. We should learn to come to the Word as little children.

Jesus said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children.” The wise and the clever are not necessarily hypocrites or enemies. There are many of God’s own dear children who neglect to cultivate a childlike spirit continually. Without realising it, they rest on how scriptural their creed is, or how honest their spiritual study is; and so the truth is hidden from them, and they never become spiritual people. “For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.” Let a deep sense of our ignorance, and a deep distrust of our own power to understand even the things of God, mark our Bible study.

The deeper our despair of ever entering fully into God’s thoughts, the greater our confident expectation can be. God wants to make His Word true in us. “Your children shall be taught by the LORD.” The Holy Spirit is already in us to reveal the things of God. In answer to our humble, believing prayer, God will give us through Him an ever-growing insight into the mystery of God — our wonderful union with Christ and likeness to Him, His living in us, and our being as He was in this world.

Yes, more: if our hearts thirst and wait for it, a time may come when, through a special outpouring of His Spirit, all our longings are satisfied, and Christ so takes possession of the heart that what was long a matter of faith becomes an experience — that as the heavens are higher than the earth, His thoughts are higher than our thoughts.
