fields.title: Meditation
fields.body_html:
“Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night” Psalms 1: 1-2.

(Joshua 1: 8. Psalms 119: 15, 23, 48, 78, 97, 99 and 148. 1 Timothy 4: 15.) “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD” Psalms 19: 14 and 49:3.

The true aim of education, study and reading lies not in what is put into us, but in what is drawn out of us, as our inner powers are awakened into active use. This is as true of studying the Bible as of any other study. God’s Word only brings its true blessing when the truth it brings us has stirred our inner life and reproduced itself in resolve, trust, love or adoration. When the heart has received the Word through the mind, and its spiritual powers have been called out and exercised on it, the Word has not returned void but has done what God sent it to do. It has become part of our life and has strengthened us for new purpose and effort.

It is in meditation that the heart holds on to the Word and makes it its own. Just as in reflection the understanding grasps the full meaning and bearings of a truth, so in meditation the heart absorbs it and makes it part of its own life. We need to be reminded continually that the heart means the will and the affections. Meditation of the heart involves desire, acceptance, surrender and love. Out of the heart flow the springs of life; what the heart truly believes, it receives with love and joy and allows to master and rule the life. The intellect gathers and prepares the food we are to live on. In meditation, the heart takes it in and feeds on it.

The art of meditation needs to be cultivated. Just as a person needs training to concentrate his mental powers so that he can think clearly and accurately, a Christian needs to reflect and meditate carefully until the holy habit has been formed of opening the whole heart to every word of God.

People sometimes ask how this power of meditation can be cultivated. The very first thing is to present ourselves before God. It is His Word, and that Word has no power to bless apart from Him. It is meant to bring us into His presence and fellowship. Practise His presence, and take the Word as coming from Him, with the assurance that He will make it work effectively in your heart. In Psalm 119 you find the word “meditate” seven times, but each time as part of a prayer addressed to God. “I will meditate on your precepts.” “Oh, how I love Your law!

All-day long it is my meditation.” Meditation is the heart turning towards God with His own Word, seeking to take it up into its affections and will, into its very life.

Another element of true meditation is quiet restfulness. In studying Scripture, as we try to follow an argument or master a difficulty, our intellect often has to make its utmost effort. The attitude of soul needed in meditation is different. Here we turn to God with some truth we have found, or some mystery on which we are waiting for divine teaching. We hide the word we are dwelling on in the depths of our heart, and believe that by the Holy Spirit its meaning and power will be revealed in our inner life.

“Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom.” In the description of our Lord’s mother we are told: “Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.” In His mother, keeping all these sayings in her heart, we have a picture of a soul that has begun to know Christ and is on the sure road to knowing Him better. It hardly needs saying that in meditation, personal application takes a leading place.

In our intellectual study of the Bible this is far too seldom the case. Its aim is to know and understand. In meditation, the chief aim is to make the truth our own and experience it. The only true spirit of Bible study is a readiness to believe every promise without reserve, to obey every command without hesitation, and to “stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.”

It is in quiet meditation that this faith is exercised, this allegiance given and this full surrender to all God’s will made, and that the assurance is received of grace to carry out our vows.

And then meditation must lead to prayer. It provides material for prayer. It must lead on to prayer — to asking for, and definitely receiving, what it has seen or accepted in the Word. Its value is that it prepares us for prayer: deliberate, wholehearted pleading for what the heart has felt the Word reveals to be needed or possible. This means that the rest of faith looks upward, confident that the Word will open up and prove its power in the soul that meekly and patiently gives itself up to it.

If we rest for a while from intellectual effort and cultivate the habit of holy meditation, the reward will be that in time the two are brought into harmony, and all our study is filled with the spirit of quiet waiting on God and of yielding our heart and life to the Word.

Our fellowship with God is meant for the whole day. The blessing of forming a habit of true meditation in the Morning Watch will be that we are brought nearer to the blessedness of the man in the first Psalm: “His delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law, he meditates day and night.”

Let all workers and leaders among God’s people remember that they need this more than others, if they are to train others in it and keep their own communication with the only source of strength and blessing unbroken. God says, “I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.” “Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law... That you may have good success wherever you go. This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night… then you will have good success… Be strong and courageous.”

“Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.” Let nothing less be your aim than that your meditation may be acceptable in His sight — part of the spiritual sacrifice you offer. Let nothing less be your prayer and expectation than that your meditation may be true worship: the living surrender of the heart to God’s Word in His presence.

fields.title: Revealed to Babies
fields.body_html:
“I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children.” Matthew 11: 25, Luke 10: 21.

The wise and clever are those who are conscious of their powers of mind and reason, and confident that these will help them in their pursuit of divine knowledge. The children are those whose chief concern is not the mind and its power but the heart and its disposition. Ignorance, helplessness, dependence, meekness, teachableness, trust and love — these are the attitudes God looks for in those He teaches (Psalms 25: 9, 12, 14, 17, 20).

One of the most important parts of our devotions is the study of God’s Word. How deeply important it is that we always receive the Word in the spirit that waits for the Father to reveal its truth in us! And how important that we have the childlike — yes, the childlike — disposition to which the Father loves to make known the secrets of His love! For the wise and clever, head knowledge comes first; and from them God hides the spiritual meaning of the very thing they think they understand.

For the children, what comes first is not the head and its knowledge but the heart and its feeling — a sense of humility, love and trust. And to them God reveals, in their inner life and experience, the very thing they know they cannot understand.

The study of education tells us that there are two styles of teaching. The ordinary teacher makes passing on knowledge his chief aim, and develops the child’s abilities only so far as they help him reach that aim. The true teacher regards the amount of knowledge as secondary.

His first aim is to develop the powers of mind and spirit, and to help the pupil, both mentally and morally, to use those powers rightly in gaining and applying knowledge. In the same way there are two kinds of preachers. Some pour out instruction, argument and appeal without end, leaving their hearers to make the best use they can of what is brought to them.

The true preacher knows how much depends on the state of the heart. Like our Lord Jesus, he seeks to make the teaching of objective truth or doctrine serve the cultivation of those dispositions without which teaching does little good. A hundred eloquent and earnest sermons to the wise and clever — to Christians who listen thinking that they can understand, and that what they hear will somehow do them good — will bring less real blessing than one sermon to hearers in whom the preacher has awakened a sense of spiritual ignorance: a childlike, teachable spirit that waits for the Father’s teaching and depends on it, and truly accepts and obeys it.

In the secret chamber, as far as human help is concerned, every person is his own teacher and preacher. He is to train himself in the blessed habit of childlike simplicity and teachableness.

He remembers that it was not enough for divine truth to be revealed in the world; there must also be a personal revelation to each one by the Holy Spirit. So his first care is to wait on the Father to reveal to him, and within him, the hidden mystery in its power in the inner life. In this posture he exercises the childlike spirit and receives the kingdom as a little child. All evangelical Christians believe in regeneration.

But how few believe that when someone is born of God, a childlike dependence on God for all teaching and strength ought to be his chief characteristic! This was the one thing our Lord Jesus insisted on above all. When He called the poor in spirit, the meek and the hungry “blessed”; when He called people to learn from Him because He was meek and lowly in heart; when He spoke so often of humbling ourselves and becoming like little children — it was because the first and chief mark of being a child of God, of being like Jesus Christ, is absolute dependence on God for every blessing, and especially for any real knowledge of spiritual things. Let each of us ask himself: Have I treated the childlike spirit as the first essential in my Bible study? What use is Bible study without the childlike spirit? It is the true and only key to God’s school.

Would it not be wise to set everything aside to secure this? Only then will God reveal His hidden wisdom.

The new birth — being born of God, by which we become God’s children — is meant to make us little children. It will give us a child’s spirit as well as a child’s teaching; it cannot give the second without the first. Let us believe in the new life within us and yield ourselves to it and to the leading of the Spirit; He will breathe into us the spirit of little children. The first aim of Bible study is to learn the hidden wisdom of God. The first condition of gaining this knowledge is to accept the fact that God Himself reveals it to us.

The first disposition needed to receive that revelation is a childlike spirit. We all know that the first thing a wise workman does is make sure he has the proper tools and that they are in good order. He does not count it lost time to stop his work and sharpen his tools. It is not lost time to let your Bible study wait until you see whether you are in the right position — waiting for the Father’s revelation in a meek and childlike spirit.

If you feel that you have not been reading your Bible in this spirit, confess and give up at once the self-confident spirit of the wise and clever. Do not only pray for the childlike spirit; believe for it. It is in you, though it has been neglected and held down; you can begin at once, as a child of God, to experience it.

Do not try to bring this childlike spirit into your heart by reflection or argument. Work from the inside outward.

It is in you as a seed, in the new life born of the Spirit. It must rise and grow in you as something born of the indwelling Spirit. In this faith you must not only pray, but pray very particularly for this grace of the Spirit, and put it into practice. Live as a little child before God. Like a newborn baby, long for the milk of the Word. And beware of trying to put on this frame of mind only when you want to study Scripture. It must be the permanent habit of your mind and the settled state of your heart. Only then can you enjoy the continual guidance of the Holy Spirit.

In the secret chamber, as far as human help is concerned, every person is his own teacher and preacher. He is to train himself in the blessed habit of childlike simplicity and teachableness. He remembers that it was not enough for divine truth to be revealed in the world; there must also be a personal revelation to each one by the Holy Spirit. So his first care is to wait on the Father to reveal to him, and within him, the hidden mystery in its power in the inner life. In this posture he exercises the childlike spirit and receives the kingdom as a little child. All evangelical Christians believe in regeneration. But how few believe that when someone is born of God, a childlike dependence on God for all teaching and strength ought to be his chief characteristic! This was the one thing our Lord Jesus insisted on above all. When He called the poor in spirit, the meek and the hungry “blessed”; when He called people to learn from Him because He was meek and lowly in heart; when He spoke so often of humbling ourselves and becoming like little children — it was because the first and chief mark of being a child of God, of being like Jesus Christ, is absolute dependence on God for every blessing, and especially for any real knowledge of spiritual things. Let each of us ask himself: Have I treated the childlike spirit as the first essential in my Bible study? What use is Bible study without the childlike spirit? It is the true and only key to God’s school. Would it not be wise to set everything aside to secure this? Only then will God reveal His hidden wisdom. The new birth — being born of God, by which we become God’s children — is meant to make us little children. It will give us a child’s spirit as well as a child’s teaching; it cannot give the second without the first. Let us believe in the new life within us and yield ourselves to it and to the leading of the Spirit; He will breathe into us the spirit of little children. The first aim of Bible study is to learn the hidden wisdom of God. The first condition of gaining this knowledge is to accept the fact that God Himself reveals it to us. The first disposition needed to receive that revelation is a childlike spirit. We all know that the first thing a wise workman does is make sure he has the proper tools and that they are in good order. He does not count it lost time to stop his work and sharpen his tools. fields.title: Learning of Christ
fields.body_html:
“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” Matthew 11: 29.

All Bible study is learning. To be fruitful, all Bible study should be learning from Christ. The Bible is the textbook; Christ is the Teacher. It is He who opens the understanding, opens the heart and opens the seals (Luke 24: 45, Acts 16: 14, Revelation 5: 9).

Christ is the living, eternal Word, and the written words are its human expression. Christ’s presence and teaching are the secret of all true Bible study. The written Word is powerless except as it helps us to the Living Word. No one has ever thought of accusing our Lord of failing to honour the Old Testament. In His own life He proved that He loved it as coming from the mouth of God. He always pointed the Jews to it as God’s revelation and the witness to Himself. But it is remarkable how often, with His disciples, He spoke of His own teaching as what they most needed and had to obey.

It was only after His resurrection — when their union with Himself had been brought about, and they had already received the first breath of the Spirit — that we find Him explaining the Scriptures.

The Jews had their own man-made interpretation of the Word, and they made it the greatest barrier between themselves and the One it spoke of. It is often the same with Christians: our human understanding of Scripture, however strongly backed by the authority of the Church or of our own circle, becomes the greatest obstacle in the way of Christ’s teaching. Christ, the Living Word, seeks first to find His place in our heart and life and to be our only Teacher; in this way we will learn from Him to honour and understand Scripture. “Learn of Me for I am meek and lowly of heart.” Here our Lord opens up the innermost secret of His own inner life. What He brought down to us from heaven, what makes Him fit to be a Teacher and a Saviour, what He has given to us and wants us to learn from Him — you find it all in the words, “I am meek and lowly of heart.” This is the one virtue that makes Him the Lamb of God, our suffering Redeemer, our heavenly Teacher and Leader. It is the one disposition He asks of us when we come to learn from Him: everything else will grow out of it.

For our Bible study and for our whole Christian life, here is the one condition of truly learning from Christ. He, the Teacher who is meek and lowly of heart, wants to make you what He is, because that is salvation.

As a learner, you must come to Him, study Him and believe in Him, the meek and lowly One, and seek to learn from Him how to be meek and lowly too. And why is this the first and all-important thing?

Because it lies at the root of the true relationship of the creature to God. God alone has life, goodness and happiness.

As the God of love, He delights to give everything and to work everything in us.

Christ became the Son of Man to show in what blessed, unceasing dependence on God man is to live: this is what His being lowly in heart means. It is in this spirit that angels veil their faces and throw their crowns down before God. God is everything to them, and they delight to receive everything and to give everything. This is the root of the true Christian life: to be nothing before God and people; to wait on God alone; to delight in Christ, the meek and lowly One, to imitate Him and to learn from Him. This is the very key to the knowledge of Scripture. Only in this character can you learn from Him. How small a place humility — the meek and lowly heart — has had in the Christian Church, compared with the place it has in the life of Christ and the teaching of God’s Word!

I am deeply convinced that this lack lies at the root of a great deal of the weakness and fruitlessness we hear about. Only as we are meek and lowly in heart can Christ teach us by His Spirit what God has for us, and will God work in us. Let each of us begin with ourselves, and treat this as the first condition of discipleship and the first lesson the Master will most surely teach us. Let us make all our Bible study a learning from Christ — trusting Him who is so meek and gentle and kind, and waiting for Him to work His own Spirit and likeness in us.

In due time our Morning Watch will become the place of daily fellowship and daily blessing.

I know the difficulties I am up against in pleading for the meek and lowly heart to be the first consideration in Bible study. It is hard to make people realise that in fellowship with God, disposition and character are everything. It is harder to show them that, of all Christian dispositions and traits of character, a meek and lowly heart is the very seed and root. It is hard to convince them that without it Bible study does very little good. Above all, it is hard to lead them to understand and believe that the meek and lowly heart can be had, because it is the very thing Christ offers to give, as He teaches us how to find it and receive it in Himself.

In the face of all these difficulties, I nevertheless urge all Bible students to consider, thoughtfully and prayerfully, whether this is not the very first question to be settled in the inner chamber: Is my heart in the state my Teacher wants it to be? And if it is not, is not my first task to yield myself to Him, so that He can work it in me?

fields.title: Teachableness
fields.body_html:
“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” — Matthew 11: 29.

The first virtue of a pupil is teachableness — a willingness to be taught. What does this involve? An awareness of his own ignorance; a readiness to give up his own way of thinking or doing, and to look at things from the teacher’s point of view; and a quiet confidence that the master knows, and will show him how he too can come to know. The meek and lowly spirit listens carefully to find out what the teacher wants, and at once hurries to carry it out. If a pupil has this spirit, it must be the teacher’s fault if he does not learn.

Why is it, then, that with Christ as our Teacher there is so much failure and so little real growth in spiritual knowledge? So much hearing and reading of the Bible, so much professed faith in it as our only rule of life, and yet so little sign of its spirit and power? Often so much honest, earnest effort in the secret place and in the Bible circle, and yet so little of the joy and strength God’s Word could give?

The question is of the greatest importance. There must be some reason why so many disciples of Jesus, who believe they honestly want to know and do His will, are still — by their own admission and in the eyes of those around them — not holding out the word of life as a light in the world. If the answer to this question could be found, their lives might be changed.

Our text suggests the answer: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” Many have taken Christ as Saviour but not as Teacher. They have put their trust in Him as the Good Shepherd who gave His life for the sheep, but they know little of the reality of His shepherding His flock day by day, calling each one by name — or of hearing His voice in this way and following Him alone. They know little of what it is to follow the Lamb: to receive from Him, before everything else, the Lamb’s nature, and to seek to be meek and lowly in heart as He is. It was through three years in His school that Christ’s disciples were made ready for the baptism of the Holy Spirit and for the fulfilment of all the wonderful promises He had given them.

It is under the personal teaching of our Lord Jesus — through the teachableness of a meek and lowly heart that waits for that teaching every day, receives it and follows it — that we can truly find rest for our souls. All the weariness and burden of strain, failure and disappointment then give way to that divine peace which knows that everything is being cared for by Christ Himself.

Taking Christ’s yoke, learning from Him His meekness and lowliness of heart, and with it the teachableness that refuses to know or do anything in its own wisdom — this is to be the spirit of our whole life, every day and all day long. But it is especially in the morning hour that this must be cultivated, and that we must seek deliverance from self and all its energy. It is there, as we are occupied with the words of God, of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, that we need to realise daily that these only do us good as they lead us to the personal teaching of Christ and are opened up by it.

It is there that we need to learn by daily experience that only when the living Lord Jesus — “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells,” the One in whom all our life and salvation are gathered up — Himself comes near and takes charge of us can His teaching be received. And it is there that we must definitely ask for, and cultivate, the teachableness that takes up His yoke and learns from Him. Once again, teachableness is everything. If it is true of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, the Spirit of Christ Jesus, that “He will teach you all things,” and if His whole life and work in us is a divine teaching, then it is equally true that our whole life must be a divine teachableness. Only in this way can our daily contact with God’s Word, and our daily life, be what our Lord Jesus can make them.

Unlearning is often the most important part of learning. Wrong impressions, prejudices and assumptions are insurmountable obstacles to learning. Until they have been removed, the teacher works in vain.

The knowledge he passes on only touches the surface; deep below the surface, the pupil is still guided by what has become second nature to him. The teacher’s first task is to discover these hindrances and to make the pupil see them and remove them.

There can be no true and fruitful learning from Christ unless we are ready to unlearn. Through heredity, education and tradition we have our own ideas about religion and God’s Word, and the surer we are that they are the truth, the greater a hindrance they often are. Learning from Christ requires a willingness to submit every truth we hold to His inspection, for criticism and correction. Humility is the root virtue of the Christian life. The law in God’s kingdom is absolute: “He who humbles himself will be exalted.” All our disappointment in striving for higher degrees of grace, faith, spiritual knowledge, love for souls and power to bless comes from this: we have not accepted the humility of Christ as the beginning and the completion of His salvation. “Gives grace to the humble” has a far wider and deeper application than we think.

Teachableness is one form of humility. In the Morning Watch we put ourselves as learners in Christ’s school. Let teachableness — let humility — be the distinguishing mark of the learner. And if we feel how little of it we have, let us listen to the voice that says, “Take My yoke upon you,” and, with all that this means: “learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”

fields.title: The Life and the Light
fields.body_html:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. In him was life, and the life was the light of men.” John 1: 1, 4.

“Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, ‘I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.’” John 8: 12.

Because Christ was God, He could be the Word of God. Because He had the life of God in Himself, He could reveal that life. And so, as the Living Word, He is the life-giving Word. The written Word can be emptied of its power and made of no effect where human wisdom is relied on to grasp it. Only when it is accepted as the seed in which the life of the Living Word lies hidden, waiting to be brought to life by the Holy Spirit, can it be the word of life to us. Our dealings with God’s written Word ought always to be inspired and governed by faith in the eternal Word, who was God.

The same truth comes out in the phrase that follows: the life is the light. When we see a light shining, we know there is a fire burning in some form or other. It is the same in the spiritual world.

There must be life where there is to be light. There may be light reflected from a dead or dark object. There may be borrowed light without life. But only true life can show true light. Whoever follows Christ will have the light of life.

These two statements of one great truth strikingly confirm what we learned about the Spirit of God. Just as the Spirit knows the things of God because He is the life of God, so Christ is the Word because He is God and has the life of God; and so the light of God shines only where the life of God is. All three thoughts bring us back to our Bible study with one blessed but much-needed lesson. Our study of Scripture can really bless us only as the written Word brings us the life of the eternal Word; only as its light within the heart is the shining of a life that is at work there; only as the Holy Spirit — who knows the things of God because He is the life of God — makes them life and truth within us.

And so we come back to the one great lesson the Spirit seeks to press home about God’s Word: there is real knowledge of Scripture only when it is received out of the life of God into our life.

It is a seed that carries the divine life within it. Where it is received in the good soil of a heart that hungers for that life, it will spring up and bear fruit, like every seed, “after its kind.”

It will reproduce in our life the very life of God it came from — the very likeness and disposition of the Father and the Son, through the Holy Spirit. We want to put all this to practical use, and apply it directly to our private Bible reading.

You want to know how to begin. The rules are very simple.

The first is: “Be still, and know that I am God.” Take time to be quiet and to become aware of God. “Be silent before the Lord GOD!” “Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD.” “But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.” Worship Him, and wait on Him so that He may speak to you. The next: remember that the Word comes out of the life and heart of God, carrying His life to pass it on to yours. It is nothing less than the life of God; nothing less than the power of God can make it live in you. The next: believe in Christ, the Living Word. “In him was life, and the life was the light of men.” “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” Follow Jesus in love and longing, in obedience and service, and so His life will work in you, and that life will be the light of your soul.

And then ask the Father for the Holy Spirit, who alone knows the things of God, to make the Word living and active in your heart. Hunger for the will of God as your daily food; thirst for the living spring of the Spirit within you; take the Word into your will, your life and your joy — and the life it brings will give the light it shines with. The reason I have insisted so often on the truth set out in these last few chapters is very simple.

My own experience has taught me how long it takes before we clearly grasp that the Word of God must be received into the life and not only into the mind — and how long again, even after we have grasped it, before we fully believe it and act on it. “To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.”

Study the lesson until you know it. The Word comes out of the life of God, carries that life within itself, and seeks to enter my life and fill it with the life of God. This life is the light of men, and gives the light of the knowledge of the glory of God. You may find that this lesson takes longer than you expect, that it seems to hinder your Bible study more than it helps, and that the longer you study it, the harder it becomes. Do not be afraid or impatient. Be assured that if you learn it properly, you will bless God that it has become a key you never had before to the hidden treasure of the Word, giving you true wisdom in the hidden part.

So I repeat once more these simple words, so endlessly blessed and true. Just as only the Spirit who lives in God knows the things of God, so only the Spirit living in me can make me know the things of God, by imparting them to my life.

Just as Christ was the Word because He was God and had the life of God, so the written Word can bless me only as the Living Word brings the life of God to me through it. Just as the life was in Christ, and the life is the light of men, so only as I have the life of Christ through the Word do I have the light of the knowledge of God.

Where it is received in the good soil of a heart that hungers for that life, it will spring up and bear fruit, like every seed, “after its kind.” It will reproduce in our life the very life of God it came from — the very likeness and disposition of the Father and the Son, through the Holy Spirit. We want to put all this to practical use, and apply it directly to our private Bible reading. You want to know how to begin. The rules are very simple. The first is: “Be still, and know that I am God.” Take time to be quiet and to become aware of God. “Be silent before the Lord GOD!” “Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD.” “But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.” Worship Him, and wait on Him so that He may speak to you. The next: remember that the Word comes out of the life and heart of God, carrying His life to pass it on to yours. It is nothing less than the life of God; nothing less than the power of God can make it live in you. The next: believe in Christ, the Living Word. “In him was life, and the life was the light of men.” “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” Follow Jesus in love and longing, in obedience and service, and so His life will work in you, and that life will be the light of your soul. And then ask the Father for the Holy Spirit, who alone knows the things of God, to make the Word living and active in your heart. Hunger for the will of God as your daily food; thirst for the living spring of the Spirit within you; take the Word into your will, your life and your joy — and the life it brings will give the light it shines with. The reason I have insisted so often on the truth set out in these last few chapters is very simple. My own experience has taught me how long it takes before we clearly grasp that the Word of God must be received into the life and not only into the mind — and how long again, even after we have grasped it, before we fully believe it and act on it. “To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.” Study the lesson until you know it. The Word comes out of the life of God, carries that life within itself, and seeks to enter my life and fill it with the life of God. This life is the light of men, and gives the light of the knowledge of the glory of God. You may find that this lesson takes longer than you expect, that it seems to hinder your Bible study more than it helps, and that the longer you study it, the harder it becomes. Do not be afraid or impatient. Be assured that if you learn it properly, you will bless God that it has become a key you never had before to the hidden treasure of the Word, giving you true wisdom in the hidden part. So I repeat once more these simple words, so endlessly blessed and true. Just as only the Spirit who lives in God knows the things of God, so only the Spirit living in me can make me know the things of God, by imparting them to my life. Just as Christ was the Word because He was God and had the life of God, so the written Word can bless me only as the Living Word brings the life of God to me through it. Just as the life was in Christ, and the life is the light of men, so only as I have the life of Christ through the Word do I have the light of the knowledge of God.

fields.title: The Bible Student
fields.body_html:
“But his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night.” Psalms 1: 2. On every side there is a loud call for more Bible study, and for truer Bible study. Evangelists like Mr. Moody and many others have shown what power there is in preaching drawn directly from God’s Word and inspired by faith in its power. Earnest Christians have asked, “Why can’t our ministers speak in the same way, giving the very Word of God a larger place?” Many young ministers have come away from theological college admitting that they were taught everything except how to study the Word for themselves, and then how to stir up and help others to study it.

In some of our churches, people have expressed the wish to meet this need in the training of ministers. It might seem a very simple matter to find good men to take on the work. And yet it has proved difficult for men with theological training to turn to the simplicity and directness of appeal to God’s Word that is needed to show younger men how to make Scripture the one source of their knowledge and teaching. In the student movement of our day — God be praised —

Bible study has been given a prominent place. There is a wonderful opportunity, as well as a very great need, to guide it in such a way that it brings full blessing to individual lives, by giving God’s Word its true place in the work to be done for Him. Let us look at the principles that lie beneath the call for more Bible study — principles which it must faithfully follow if it is to be carried out truly. 1. God’s Word Is the Only Authentic Revelation of God’s Will. All human statements of divine truth, however correct, are imperfect and carry only a measure of human authority. In the Word, the voice of God speaks to us directly. Every child of God is called to direct fellowship with the Father through the Word. Since God reveals all His heart and grace in it, His child — if he receives it from God — can take all the life and power that is in the Word into his own heart and being. We know how few second-hand reports of messages or events can be fully trusted. Very few people report accurately what they have heard. Every believer has the right and the calling to stand in direct communication with God. It is in the Word that God has revealed Himself, and it is in the Word that He still reveals Himself, to each individual.

2. This Word of God is a living word. It carries a divine, life-giving power within it. A human expression of the truth is often only an idea or image of the truth, appealing to the mind and having little or no effect. Faith that it is God’s own Word, and that His presence and power are in it, is what makes it effective. All life, all spirit, creates a form for itself in which it shows itself.

The words in which God has chosen to clothe His own divine thoughts are God-breathed, and the life of God dwells in them. God is not the God of the dead but of the living. The Word was not only inspired when it was first given; the Spirit of God still breathes in it. God is still in His Word and with it. Christians and teachers need to believe this. It will lead them to place a confidence in the simple divine Word that no human teaching may claim.

3. God Himself alone can be — and He most surely will be — the interpreter of His own Word. Divine truth needs a divine Teacher. Spiritual understanding of spiritual things can only come from the Holy Spirit. The deeper our conviction of the unique character of the Word — essentially different from all merely human understanding and infinitely exalted above it — the more urgently we will feel the need for supernatural, directly divine teaching. And all the more will the great purpose of the Word be fulfilled in blessing. The soul will be brought to seek God Himself, and will be led to find Him in the Holy Spirit who dwells in the heart. In that Spirit, God has so wonderfully entered our very life and made Himself one with it. As we wait on Him and trust Him, He will make us know wisdom in the hidden part — in the heart and the disposition. The Word, read prayerfully and treasured in the heart in this faith, will become both light and life within us through the Spirit.

4. So the Word brings us into the closest and most intimate fellowship with God — a unity of will and life. In the Word God has revealed His whole heart and all His will: in His law and precepts, what He wants us to do; in His redemption and His promises, what He wants to do for us. As we accept that will in the Word as coming from God Himself, and yield ourselves to its working, we learn to know God in His will — in the power by which He works in us, and in which His condescending love is made known. And the Word carries out His richest purpose as it fills us with the reverence and dependence that come from God’s presence and nearness. Nothing less than this must be our aim, and may be our experience, in all our Bible study.

Let us now go over these four thoughts again and apply them in practice. In Holy Scripture we have the very words in which the holy God has spoken, and in which He speaks to us. These words are full of the life of God today. God is in them, and makes His presence and power known to those who seek Him there. To those who ask for and wait on the teaching of the Holy Spirit who lives within us, the Spirit will reveal the spiritual meaning and power of the Word. So the Word is meant to be, every day, the means by which God reveals Himself to the soul and by which we have fellowship with Him. Have we learned to apply these truths? Do we understand that the Word is always saying, “Seek God”? Listen to God. Wait for God. God will speak to you. Let God teach you.

All we hear about more Bible teaching and Bible study must lead to this one thing. We must be people — and we must help train others to be people — for whom the Word is never separated from the living God Himself, and who live as those to whom God in heaven speaks every day and all day long.

fields.title: Who Are You?
fields.body_html:
“Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth, For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”— Colossians 3: 2, 3.

When the Christian enters God’s presence in the morning hour, much depends on his realising not only who God is, but who he himself is, and in what relationship he stands to God. Everyone who claims the right to come near and be heard by the Most High is asked — not in words but in spirit — “Who are you?” There must be an answer ready deep within him, and that inner awareness must be nothing less than a living sense of the place he has in Christ before God. The way he puts it may differ from time to time, but in substance it will always be the same.

Who am I? Yes, let me think about it and say it: who am I to ask God to meet me here and spend this whole day with me? I am someone who knows, by the Word and Spirit of God, that I am in Christ, and that my life is hidden with Christ in God. In Christ I died to sin and to the world. I have now been taken out of them, separated from them and set free from their power. I have been raised together with Christ, and in Him I live to God.

My life is hidden with Christ in God, and I come to God to claim and receive all the divine life that is stored up in Him to supply today’s needs.

Yes, this is who I am. I say it to God, with humble, holy reverence, as my plea. I say it to myself, to encourage others as well as myself to seek and expect nothing less than grace to live out here on earth the hidden life of heaven. I am someone who longs to say — and who does say — Christ is my life. My soul longs for Christ, revealed by the Father Himself within the heart. Nothing less can satisfy me. My life is hidden with Christ. He can be my life in no other way than by being in my heart. Yes! I can be content with nothing less than Christ in the heart.

Christ, a Saviour from sin. Christ, the gift and the bringer of God’s love. Christ, an indwelling Friend and Lord. O my God, if You ask, “Who are you?” listen to my stammering: I live in Christ, and Christ lives in me. You alone can make me know all that this means, and be all that it means. There is more I will have to say as my plea for the grace of God’s presence and power all day long. I come as someone who desires and seeks to be made ready to live out the life of Christ on earth today — to translate His hidden, heavenly glory into the language of daily life, with its attitudes and its duties.

As Christ on earth lived only to do the will of God, so it is my great desire to stand perfect and complete in all His will.

My ignorance of that will, in all its spiritual application to my dealings with the world and with people, is very great. My helplessness is greater still. And yet I come to God as one who dares not offer less or look for any compromise — as one who, in all honesty, accepts the high calling of living out the will of God fully in all things.

This is what brings me to the secret place. As I think of all my failures to fulfil God’s will, as I look ahead to all the temptations and dangers waiting for me, as I feel how completely inadequate I am, and yet say to God, I come to claim the life hidden in Christ so that I may live the life for Christ — I feel urged and drawn not to be content without the quiet assurance that God will go with me and bless me.

Who am I to ask such great and wonderful things of God? May I really expect to live the life hidden with Christ in God, so as to make it visible in my mortal body? I may, for it is God Himself who will work it in me by the Holy Spirit living in me. The same God who raised Christ from the dead and then seated Him at His right hand has raised me with Him, and has given me the Spirit of His Son’s glory in my heart.

A life in Christ, given up to knowing and doing all God’s will, is the life God Himself will work and keep up in me more and more by the Holy Spirit. And when I come in the morning and present myself before Him — to take up afresh the life He has hidden in Himself for me, where His Son is hidden, and to live it out in the flesh — I can wait, confidently and quietly, as one in whom the Spirit lives, for the Father to give the fresh anointing that teaches all things, and to take charge Himself of the new day He has given me.

My brother, I am sure you feel how infinitely important it is, if the morning hour is to secure God’s presence for the day, that you take your firm stand on nothing less than the ground of full redemption.

Believe what God says to you. Accept what God has given you in Christ. Be, consciously and openly, what God has made you to be. Take time before God to know it and to say it. How much in a battle depends on holding a position that cannot be taken! Take your place where God has put you.

At times the very effort to do this may interfere with your ordinary Bible study or prayer. It will be no loss; it will be fully repaid later. Your whole life depends on knowing who your God is, and who you are as His redeemed one in Christ. Every day’s life depends on it. Once you have learned the secret, it will be the strength of your heart, even when you are not thinking of it — both as you go in to God and as you go out with Him into the world.

fields.title: The Will of God
fields.body_html:
“Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.”— Matthew 6: 10.

1. The will of God is the living power to which the world owes its existence. It is through that will, and in keeping with that will, that the world is what it is. The world is the expression, the display, the embodiment of the divine will in its wisdom, power and goodness. All its beauty and glory it owes simply to God having willed it. As that will formed it, so it upholds it every day. In this way creation does what it was made for: it shows the glory of God. “The living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, for you created all things, and by your will, they existed and were created.”

2. This is true of lifeless nature. It is even more true of intelligent creatures. The divine will set out to create a being in its own image and likeness, with the living power to know, accept and work together with the will to which it owed its existence. The blessedness of the unfallen angels lies in counting it their highest honour and happiness to be able to will and do exactly what God wills and does. The glory of heaven is that God’s will is done there.

The sin and misery of fallen angels and of fallen humanity consist simply in this: they have turned away from the will of God, and refused to remain in it and to do it.

3. Redemption is nothing other than the restoring of God’s will to its place in the world. For this purpose Christ came and showed, in a human life, that man has only one thing to live for — doing God’s will. He showed us that there was one way of conquering self-will: by dying to it, in obeying God’s will even to death. In this way He atoned for our self-will and conquered it for us, and opened a path through death and resurrection into a life wholly united with the will of God and devoted to it.

4. God’s redeeming will is now able to do in fallen man what His creating will has done, and always does, in nature and in unfallen beings. In Christ and His example, God has revealed the devotion to His will, and the delight in it, that He asks and expects of us. In Christ and by His Spirit He renews our will and takes possession of it: He works in it both to will and to do, making us able and willing to do all His will. He Himself works all things according to the counsel of His will. “Equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight.” As this is revealed by the Holy Spirit, believed and received into the heart, we begin to gain insight into the prayer, “Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven,” and a true desire is awakened for the life it promises.

5. How essential it is for the believer to grasp his relationship to God’s will and the claim it makes on him! Very many believers have no idea what their faith or their feelings ought to be with regard to the will of God. How few say: My whole idea of blessedness is nothing but the most complete harmony with the will of God. I feel that my one need is a surrender that is constantly maintained — never, in the very smallest thing, to do anything other than what God wills me to do. By God’s grace, every hour of my life can be lived in the will of God, doing it as it is done in heaven.

6. Only as a living faith in the divine will, working out its purposes more and more in us, takes control of the heart will we have the courage to believe in the answer to the prayer our Lord taught us. Only as we see that it is through Jesus Christ that God’s will is carried out in us will we understand how it is close union with Him that gives the confidence that God will work everything in us. And only this confidence in God, through Jesus Christ, will assure us that we too can do our part, and that our feeble will on earth can truly match and work together with the will of God. Let us accept our destiny and our obligation as the one thing our heart desires: that in everything the will of God may be done in us and by us as it is done in heaven. That faith will overcome the world.

7. The will must not be cut off from its living union with the Father here, nor from the living presence of the blessed Son. Only by divine guidance, given through the Holy Spirit, can the will of God be truly known — in its beauty, in its application to daily life and in its ever-growing revelation. This teaching will be given not to the wise and clever but to little children — people of a childlike disposition who are willing to wait for what is given them and to depend on it. The divine guidance will lead in the path of God’s will.

8. Our secret fellowship with God is the place where we repeat and learn the great lessons… the God I worship asks of me perfect union with His will… My worship means: “I delight to do your will, O my God.” In the morning hour, in the inner chamber, in secret fellowship with God, we seek and cultivate the knowledge of God’s will, the power to do it and the complete and joyful surrender to do all that God wills. As we do, our study of God’s Word and our prayer will bring their true and full blessing.

fields.title: Feeding on the Word
fields.body_html:
“Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart” — Jeremiah 15: 16.

Here you have three things. First, the finding of God’s words. This comes only to those who search diligently for them. Then the eating. This means making them personally our own for our nourishment — taking the words of God up into our very being. “But he answered, ‘It is written, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.”’” Matthew 4:4. And then the rejoicing: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy, he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.” Matthew 13:44. There we have the finding, the making our own and the rejoicing. “Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart.”

Eating is the central thought here. Searching and finding come before it; rejoicing goes with it and follows it. It is the only aim and purpose of the first, and the only cause and life of the second. In the secrecy of the inner chamber, how much depends on this — I did eat them!

To see the difference between this and the finding of God’s words, compare the grain a man may have stored in his barn with the bread he has on his table. All the hard work he has put into sowing, harvesting and storing his grain, and all the rich reward his care has brought him, can do him no good unless he feeds on the daily portion of bread his body needs. In the finding — the harvesting and storing — what mattered was the greater the quantity and the quicker the work, the better. In the eating, it is just the opposite: here it is the small quantity, and the slow, unbroken continuance, that mark the process of making it our own.

Do you see how this applies to your study of Scripture in the Morning Watch? You need to find God’s words and master them by careful thought, so that you have them stored in your mind and memory for your own use. And there is great joy in this — the joy of harvest or of victory, the joy of treasure secured or difficulties overcome. And yet we must remember that finding and possessing the words of God is not yet the eating of them, which alone brings divine life and strength to the soul.

Being busy with good, wholesome grain, and owning it, will not nourish a man. Being deeply interested in the knowledge of God’s Word will not, in itself, nourish the soul. “Your words were found” — that was the first thing. “And I ate them” — that is what brought joy and rejoicing.

And what is this eating? The grain the farmer had grown, and rejoiced in as his very own, could not nourish his life until he took it and ate it — until he absorbed it so completely that it became part of himself, entering his blood and forming his very bone and flesh. This has to be done in small amounts at a time, two or three times a day, every day of the year. This is the law of eating. It is not how interesting or successful my Bible study is, nor how much clearer my view or wider my grasp is becoming, that secures the health and growth of my spiritual life. Not at all. All this often leaves our nature very unsanctified and unspiritual, with very little of the holiness or humility of Christ Jesus. Something else is needed. Jesus said: My food is to do the will of him who sent me.

Take a small portion of God’s Word — some definite command or duty of the new life. Quietly receive it into your will and into the love of your heart. Yield your whole being to its rule, and vow, in the power of the Lord Jesus, to carry it out. Do this, and then go and do it: this is eating the Word — taking it into our innermost being, so that it becomes a lasting part of our very life. It is the same with a truth or a promise: what you have eaten now becomes part of you, and you carry it with you wherever you go, as part of the life you live.

You see at once how the two points of difference between the grain in the barn and the bread on the table cover the whole of your Bible study. Gathering Scripture knowledge is one thing. Eating God’s Word — receiving it into your heart by the power of the life-giving Spirit — is something quite different.

And you see how the two laws of eating food, as opposed to the laws of finding it, must always be obeyed. You can gather and store grain to last for years. You cannot swallow enough bread at once to last for days. Day by day, and more than once a day, you take your food for that day. In the same way, the eating of God’s Word must be in small portions — just as much as the soul can receive and digest each time. And this must go on day by day, from one end of the year to the other.

It is this kind of feeding on the Word that will enable me to say: “Your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart.” George Müller says he learned that he ought not to stop reading the Word until he felt happy in God; then he felt fit to go out to his day’s work.

fields.title: Holidays
fields.body_html:
“But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into.” Luke 12: 39.

In an address on education, Edward Thring says: “The mighty leisure hours with their occupations are all-powerful… The mighty question of leisure hours ought to be the most important question of all, since it affects the character most… Leisure hours are the hinge on which true education turns.” This great master of the science of education had seen that noble character and truth of being come first, and only after that, second, the training of skill and strength. He had also seen that, although a teacher can do much by word and deed — by high belief and true work — to stimulate and guide, every boy has to work out his own character. And because it is in his leisure hours, when he is free from restraint and from being watched, that a boy shows what is really uppermost in him, Thring spoke of the leisure hours as all-important and all-powerful, the hinge on which true education turns. In religion this is intensely true.

Thousands of students have felt it without knowing how to put it into words or explain it.

At college or school, their Morning Watch has had its place in the timetable. The whole mind is geared to regular, systematic work, and the time for devotion is kept as faithfully as the time for a class or for private study.

Then the holidays come, and you are free to do exactly as you like. And many find that the Morning Watch and its fellowship with God had not become so natural, so necessary to the spiritual life or so full of joy that keeping it could hold its own against holiday pleasures. The holiday becomes the test of character — the proof of how far one can say with Job, “I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.” The question of leisure hours really is all-important. In them I turn freely and naturally to what I love most. In them I prove, and increase, my power to hold on to what I have.

A teacher in a large school in America is reported to have said, “The greatest difficulty we have to contend with is the summer vacation. Just when we have brought a boy up to a good level of discipline, and he is responding to the best ideals, we lose him, and when he comes back in the autumn, we have to begin and do it all over again.

The summer holiday simply demoralises him.” This statement, about ordinary study and duty, is strong; within certain limits, it applies just as much to the religious life.

The sudden loosening of regular habits, and the subtle idea that perfect freedom to do as one likes means perfect happiness, set many a young student back in his Christian life.

There is no point at which it is more necessary for the older and more experienced members of the Students’ Association to help and guard their younger members than this. What has been gained over months can be lost through a week’s neglect. We do not know at what hour the thief will come. The spirit of the Morning Watch means unceasing watchfulness, all day and every day.

There are various ways in which the danger, and the way to be safe from it, can be put to the student. With the holidays, we are set free from the school rules we live under while we are there. But there are other laws — the laws of morality and the laws of health — from which there is no holiday. Let the student be warned that the call to daily fellowship with God belongs not to the first kind but to the second. Just as much as he needs to eat and breathe every day during the holidays, he needs Every Day to Eat the Bread and Breathe the Air of Heaven.

Make it clear that the Morning Watch is not only a duty but an inexpressible privilege and pleasure. Fellowship with God, abiding in Christ, loving the Word and meditating on it all day long — to the new nature these things are life and strength, health and gladness.

Look at them in this light. Believe in the power of the new nature within you, and act on it; even if you do not feel it, it will come true. Count it a joy, and it will become a joy to you.

Above all, realise that the world needs you and depends on you to be its light. Christ is waiting for you, as a member of His body, to do His saving work through you day by day. Neither He, nor the world, nor you can afford to lose a single day. God has created and redeemed you so that through you — as unceasingly as He lights the world through the sun — He may let His light and life and love shine out on people.

You need to be in touch with the fountain of all light every day. Do not think of asking for a holiday from this fellowship — still less of taking one. Value the holiday for the special time it gives you to study what lay outside your ordinary Bible study course. Value it for the special opportunity it gives for more fellowship with the Father and the Son. Instead of letting it become a trap, and spending all your energy just keeping yourself from losing ground, value the holiday as a blessed time of grace and of victory over self and the world, of great increase in grace and strength, of being blessed and made a blessing.

fields.title: The Inward and the Outward
fields.body_html:
“You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also?” Luke 11: 40.

Every spirit seeks to create for itself a form or shape in which its life is embodied. The outward is the visible expression of the hidden inward life. The outward is usually known before the inward; through it, the inward develops and reaches its full maturity, as the apostle says in 1 Corinthians 15: 46: “But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.” To understand and keep the right relationship between the inward and the outward is one of the greatest secrets of the Christian life.

If Adam in paradise had not listened to the tempter, his testing would have led to the maturing of his inward life. His sin, his ruin and the cause of all his misery was that he gave himself up to the power of the visible, outward world. Instead of seeking his happiness in the hidden inward life of a heart that honoured God’s command — in the inward dispositions of love and faith, of obedience and dependence — he set his desire on the world outside him, on the pleasure and the knowledge of good and evil it could give him.

All false religion, from the most degrading idolatry to the corruption of Judaism and of Christianity, has its root in this: what is outward — what can please the eye, interest the mind or gratify the taste — takes the place of that truth in the inward being, that hidden wisdom in the heart and life, which God looks for and gives.

The great mark of the New Testament is that it is an age of the inner life. The promise of the new covenant is: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts.” “And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.” The promise of our Lord Jesus was, “In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.” Religion consists in the state of the heart. True salvation is found in a heart into which God has sent the Spirit of His Son, a heart in which the love of God has been poured out.

The inner chamber, with its secret fellowship with the Father who sees in secret, is both the symbol and the training school of the inner life. Faithful, genuine daily use of the inner chamber will make the hidden inner life strong and glad.

In all our religion, the great danger is giving more time and interest to the outward means than to the inward reality. It is not the intensity of your Bible study, nor the frequency or fervour of your prayers or good works, that necessarily makes up a true spiritual life.

No! What we need is to realise that, just as God is Spirit, so there is a spirit within us that can know Him and receive Him, be shaped into His likeness, and share in the very dispositions that move Him as God in His goodness and love.

Settle this firmly in your mind: our whole salvation consists in the nature, life and spirit of Christ Jesus being made visible in our new self, outward and inward. This alone renews and recovers the original life of God in the human soul. Wherever you go and whatever you do — at home or out in the field — do everything with a desire for union with Christ, in imitation of His dispositions and inclinations. Long for nothing, and desire nothing so much, as whatever exercises and increases the spirit and life of Christ in your soul, and to have everything within you changed into the disposition and spirit of the holy Jesus.

Think of the treasure you have within you: the Saviour of the world, the eternal Word of God, hidden in your heart as a seed of the divine nature, which is to overcome sin and death within you and bring the life of heaven to birth again in your soul. Turn to your heart, and your heart will find its Saviour, its God, within itself. You see and feel nothing of God because you look for Him outside — in books, in the church, in outward exercises. But you will not find Him there until you have first found Him in your heart. Look for Him in your heart and you will never look in vain, for He lives there; there is the seat of His light and His Holy Spirit.

fields.title: The Daily Renewal — Its Power
fields.body_html:
“So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.” 2 Corinthians 4:16.

“He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” Titus 3: 5.

With every new day, the life of nature is renewed. As the sun rises again with its light and warmth, the flowers open, the birds sing, and life everywhere is stirred and strengthened. When we get up from our night’s rest and eat our morning meal, we feel we have gained new strength for the day’s duties. The inner chamber is a standing admission that our inner life needs daily renewal too. Only by fresh nourishment from God’s Word, and fresh fellowship with God Himself in prayer, can the vigour of the spiritual life be kept up and made to grow.

Though our outward self is wasting away — though the burden of sickness or suffering, the strain of work and weariness may drain us or weaken us — the inward self can be renewed day by day.

A quiet time and place, with the Word and prayer, are the means of this renewal. But they are means only when the divine power that works through them gives them life. That power is the Holy Spirit, the mighty power of God at work in us. Our study of the inner chamber, and of the inner life it stands for, would be incomplete if we did not give due place to the daily renewal of the inward self, which it is always the work of the blessed Spirit to bring about. In the text from Titus we are taught that “He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit.” The two expressions are not meant to say the same thing twice.

Regeneration is one great act, the beginning of the Christian life; the renewing of the Holy Spirit is a work that goes on continually and never ends. In Romans 12: 2 we read that the ongoing transformation of the Christian life comes by “The Renewing of the Mind.” In Ephesians 4: 23, the words “put off the old man” (in the aorist tense) point to an act done once for all; the words “Be Renewed in the Spirit of Your Mind” are in the present tense and point to an ongoing work. In the same way, in Colossians 3:10 we read, “And have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.” It is to the blessed Spirit that we are to look, and on Him that we can count, for the daily renewal of the inner self in the inner chamber.

In our secret devotions everything depends on keeping the right relationship with the adorable Third Person of the blessed Trinity. fields.title: The Daily Renewal — The Pattern
fields.body_html:
“Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices, and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.” — Colossians 3: 9-10.

“Assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus, and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.” Ephesians 4: 21, 23, 24.

In every pursuit, it matters to have the goal clearly defined. It is not enough that there is movement and progress; we want to know whether the movement is in the right direction, straight towards the mark. And especially when we are working in partnership with someone else, on whom we depend, we need to know that our aim and his are in perfect agreement. If our daily renewal is to reach its goal, we need to know clearly what its purpose is and hold firmly to it.

“You have put on the new man, which is being renewed unto knowledge.” The divine life, the work of the Holy Spirit within us, is not a blind force as in nature. We are to be fellow workers with God; our co-operation is to be intelligent and willing. “The new man is being renewed day by day unto knowledge.” There is a knowledge that the natural understanding can draw from the Word, but it lacks the life and power — the real truth and substance — that spiritual knowledge brings.

It is the renewing of the Holy Spirit that gives true knowledge. This knowledge does not consist in thoughts and ideas, but in an inward tasting — a living reception of the very things themselves, of which the words and thoughts are only pictures. “Have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge.” However diligent our Bible study may be, we gain no true knowledge beyond the point to which we are experiencing spiritual renewal. Only “the renewal in the spirit of the mind” — in its life and inner being — brings true divine knowledge.

And what is the pattern that will be revealed to this spiritual knowledge, the true and only aim that grows out of the renewal? The new man is being renewed unto knowledge, after the Image of Him That Created Him. Nothing less than the image, the likeness, of God! That is the one aim of the Holy Spirit in His daily renewing, and it must be the aim of the believer who seeks that renewing.

This was God’s purpose in creation: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.” How little we consider the infinite glory of these words! Was it not for nothing less than this that God breathed His own life into man — so that it might reproduce in man on earth a perfect likeness of God in heaven? In Christ, that image of God has been revealed and seen in human form. We have been predestined, redeemed and called; we are being taught and made fit by the Holy Spirit to be conformed to the image of the Son, to be imitators of God, and to walk just as Christ walked. How can the daily renewal go on, and what good can daily Bible study and prayer do, unless we set our hearts on what God has set His on: The New Man Being Renewed Day by Day After The Image of Him That Created Him?

In the second passage we have the same thought put a little differently. Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, which after God — according to the likeness of God — has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth. Righteousness is God’s hatred of sin and His upholding of what is right. Holiness is God’s indescribable glory in the perfect harmony of His righteousness and love — His infinite exaltation above the creature, and His perfect union with it. In man, righteousness covers all God’s will for our duty to Him or to our fellow men; holiness, our personal relationship to God Himself. As the new man has been created, so it has to be renewed daily, after God, in righteousness and holiness of truth. It is to bring this about that the power of the Holy Spirit is at work in us. It is to bring this about that He waits for us, day by day, to yield ourselves to Him in His renewing grace and power.

The morning hour, returning each day, is the time for securing the daily renewing of the Holy Spirit into the image of God, in righteousness and holiness of truth. How much we need meditation and prayer to set our hearts on what God is aiming at, and to gain a true vision of this wonderful possibility: the inward self renewed day by day into the very likeness of God, changed into the same image, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Christian student!

Let nothing less be your aim, and let nothing less satisfy your longings. The image of God, the life of God, is in you. His likeness can be seen in you. Do not separate God and His likeness any longer. Let every approach to Him, and all your trust in Him, mean nothing less than finding Him, in His likeness worked into you by the renewing of the Holy Spirit. Let this be your daily prayer: to be renewed after the image of Him who created you.

fields.title: The Daily Renewal — Its Cost
fields.body_html:
“So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.” 2 Corinthians 4: 16.

“Do not be conformed to this world but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.” Romans 12: 2.

It is no small or easy thing to be a mature, strong Christian. On God’s side, it means that it cost the Son of God His life, that it takes the mighty power of God to create a person anew, and that nothing less than the unceasing, daily care of the Holy Spirit can sustain that life.

On our side, it demands that when the new self is put on, the old self is put off. All the dispositions, habits and pleasures of our own nature that make up the life we have been living are to be put away. Everything we have through our birth from Adam must be sold, if we are to possess the pearl of great price.

If anyone is to come after Christ, he must deny himself, take up his cross, leave everything and follow Christ on the path He walked. He must throw away not only all sin, but everything — however necessary, legitimate and precious — that may become an occasion for sin: he must pluck out the eye or cut off the hand. He must hate his own life and lose it, if he is to live in “the power of an endless life.” It is a solemn thing — far more solemn than most people think — to be a true Christian.

This is especially true of the daily renewing of the inward self. Paul speaks of it as accompanied by, and dependent on, the wasting away of the outward self. The whole epistle (2 Corinthians) shows us how sharing in the sufferings of Christ, even to being conformed to His death, was the secret of his life of power and of blessing to the churches. “Always bearing about in the body the dying of Jesus, that the life also of Jesus may be manifested in our body. For we which live are always delivered unto death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh. So then death works in us, but life in you.”

The full experience of the life of Christ in our person, our body and our work for others depends on our sharing in His suffering and death. There can be no great measure of renewal of the inward self without the sacrifice — the wasting away — of the outward.

To be filled with heaven, life must be emptied of earth. We have the same truth in our second text: “Be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” An old house may be renovated and still keep much of its old appearance; or the renovation may be so complete that people exclaim, What a transformation! The renewing of the mind by the Holy Spirit means a complete transformation — an entirely different way of thinking, judging and deciding. The fleshly mind gives way to a “spiritual understanding” (Colossians 1: 9, 1 John 5: 20). This transformation is gained only at the cost of giving up everything that belongs to our natural self. “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed.”

By nature we belong to this world. When we are renewed by grace, we are still in the world, exposed to its subtle, all-pervading influence, from which we cannot withdraw. What is more, the world is still in us, like the leaven of our nature, which nothing can purge out except the mighty power of the Holy Spirit filling us with the life of heaven.

Let us allow these truths to take deep hold of us and master us. The divine transformation, by the daily renewing of our mind into the image of Him who is far above, can go on in us no faster and no further than we seek to be freed from every trace of conformity to this world. The negative, “Do not be conformed to this world,” needs to be stressed as strongly as the positive, “be transformed.” The spirit of this world and the Spirit of God are fighting for possession of our being. Only as the first is recognised, renounced and driven out can the heavenly Spirit come in and do His blessed work of renewing and transforming.

The whole world, and whatever belongs to the worldly spirit, must be given up. The whole of life, and whatever belongs to self, must be lost. This daily renewal of the inward self costs a great deal — that is, as long as we are hesitating, or trying to do it in our own strength. But once we really learn that the Holy Spirit does it all, and once we have given up everything in faith in the strength of the Lord Jesus, the renewing becomes the simple, natural, healthy and joyful growth of the heavenly life in us.

Then the inner chamber becomes the place we long for every day, where we praise God for what He has done, what He is doing and what we know He will do. Day by day we yield ourselves afresh to the blessed Lord who has said, “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’” The renewing of the Holy Spirit becomes one of the most blessed realities of our daily Christian life.
