fields.title: Holiness — The Chief Aim of Bible Study
fields.body_html:
“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” John 17: 17.

In His great prayer of intercession, our Lord spoke of the words the Father had given Him, of His giving them to His disciples, and of their receiving and believing them. It was this that made them disciples. It was by keeping these words that they would truly be able to live the life, and do the work, of real disciples. Receiving God’s words from Christ and keeping them is both the mark and the power of true discipleship.

As He prays to the Father to keep them in the world after He has left it, our Lord asks Him to sanctify them in the truth, as it dwells and works in His Word. Christ had said of Himself, “I am the truth.” He was the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. His teaching was not like the law that came through Moses, which gave a knowledge, a promise of good things to come, that was only an image or a shadow.

“The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” They give the very substance and power, the divine possession, of what they speak of. Christ had spoken of the Spirit as the Spirit of truth, who would lead them into all the truth that was in Himself — not as a matter of knowledge or doctrine, but into actually experiencing and enjoying it.

And then He prays that the Father would sanctify them in this living truth, as it dwells in the Word and is revealed in Him by the Spirit. “For their sake,” He says, “I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.” And He asks the Father, in His power and love, to take charge of them, so that His purpose — to sanctify them in the truth, through His Word, which is truth — may be fulfilled, and that they, like Himself, may be sanctified in truth. Let us study the wonderful lessons given here about God’s Word.

“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” The great purpose of God’s Word is to make us holy. No amount of diligence or success in Bible study will really profit us unless it makes us humbler and holier. In all our use of Holy Scripture, this must definitely be our main aim. The reason there is often so much Bible reading with so little real result in Christlike character is that “salvation, through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth,” is not truly sought. People imagine that if they study the Word and accept its truths, this will in some way benefit them by itself.

But experience shows that it does not. The fruit — a holy character, a consecrated life, power to bless others — does not come, for the simple and very natural reason that we only get what we seek. Christ gave us God’s Word to make us holy. Only when we make this our definite aim in all our Bible study can the truth open itself up and impart itself to us — not doctrinal truth, but its divine, life-giving power, which carries the very life of God within it as a seed.

“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” It is God Himself, and He alone, who can make us holy through His Word. The Word, separated from God and His direct working, can do nothing. The Word is an instrument: God Himself must use it. God alone is the Holy One; He alone can make holy. The inexpressible value of God’s Word is that it is God’s means of holiness. The terrible mistake many make is forgetting that only God can use it or make it effective. It is not enough to have access to a doctor’s dispensary; I need him to prescribe. Without him, my use of his medicines could be fatal. So it was with the scribes. They boasted of God’s law and delighted in studying Scripture, and yet they remained unsanctified. The Word did not sanctify them, because they did not seek this in the Word, and did not yield to God for Him to do it for them.

“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” This holiness through the Word must be sought from God in prayer, and waited for. Our Lord did not only teach His disciples that they must be holy; He did not only sanctify Himself for them, so that they might be sanctified in truth. He also brought His words and His work to the Father, with the prayer that He would sanctify them. It is very necessary to know God’s Word and to meditate on it. It is very necessary to set our hearts on being holy as our first and chief aim in studying the Word. But all this is not enough. Everything depends on our following Christ in asking the Father to sanctify us through the Word. It is God, the Holy Father, who makes us holy, by the Spirit of holiness who lives in us. He works in us the very mind and disposition of Christ, who is our sanctification. “There is none holy like the LORD”; all holiness is His, and is what He gives by His holy presence.

The tabernacle and the temple were not made holy by cleansing, separation or consecration. They became holy when God came in and dwelt there. His taking possession made them holy. In the same way, God makes us holy through His Word, as it brings Christ and the Holy Spirit into us. And the Father cannot do this unless we wait before Him and are still, and give ourselves up to Him in deep dependence and full surrender. It is in prayer offered in the name, the fellowship and the faith of the great Intercessor — “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth” — that the Father’s sanctifying power will be found, and that our knowledge of God’s Word will truly make us holy.

How sacred the Morning Watch is! This hour is set apart in a special way for the soul to yield itself up to God’s holiness, to be sanctified through the Word. Let us always remember that the one aim of God’s Word is to make us holy. Let our continual prayer be, “Father, sanctify me in your truth.”

His teaching was not like the law that came through Moses, which gave a knowledge, a promise of good things to come, that was only an image or a shadow. “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” They give the very substance and power, the divine possession, of what they speak of. Christ had spoken of the Spirit as the Spirit of truth, who would lead them into all the truth that was in Himself — not as a matter of knowledge or doctrine, but into actually experiencing and enjoying it. And then He prays that the Father would sanctify them in this living truth, as it dwells in the Word and is revealed in Him by the Spirit. “For their sake,” He says, “I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.” And He asks the Father, in His power and love, to take charge of them, so that His purpose — to sanctify them in the truth, through His Word, which is truth — may be fulfilled, and that they, like Himself, may be sanctified in truth. Let us study the wonderful lessons given here about God’s Word. “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” The great purpose of God’s Word is to make us holy. No amount of diligence or success in Bible study will really profit us unless it makes us humbler and holier. In all our use of Holy Scripture, this must definitely be our main aim. The reason there is often so much Bible reading with so little real result in Christlike character is that “salvation, through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth,” is not truly sought. People imagine that if they study the Word and accept its truths, this will in some way benefit them by itself. But experience shows that it does not. The fruit — a holy character, a consecrated life, power to bless others — does not come, for the simple and very natural reason that we only get what we seek. Christ gave us God’s Word to make us holy. Only when we make this our definite aim in all our Bible study can the truth open itself up and impart itself to us — not doctrinal truth, but its divine, life-giving power, which carries the very life of God within it as a seed. “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” It is God Himself, and He alone, who can make us holy through His Word. The Word, separated from God and His direct working, can do nothing. The Word is an instrument: God Himself must use it. God alone is the Holy One; He alone can make holy. The inexpressible value of God’s Word is that it is God’s means of holiness. The terrible mistake many make is forgetting that only God can use it or make it effective. It is not enough to have access to a doctor’s dispensary; I need him to prescribe. Without him, my use of his medicines could be fatal. So it was with the scribes. They boasted of God’s law and delighted in studying Scripture, and yet they remained unsanctified. The Word did not sanctify them, because they did not seek this in the Word, and did not yield to God for Him to do it for them. “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” This holiness through the Word must be sought from God in prayer, and waited for. Our Lord did not only teach His disciples that they must be holy; He did not only sanctify Himself for them, so that they might be sanctified in truth. He also brought His words and His work to the Father, with the prayer that He would sanctify them. It is very necessary to know God’s Word and to meditate on it. It is very necessary to set our hearts on being holy as our first and chief aim in studying the Word. But all this is not enough. Everything depends on our following Christ in asking the Father to sanctify us through the Word. It is God, the Holy Father, who makes us holy, by the Spirit of holiness who lives in us. He works in us the very mind and disposition of Christ, who is our sanctification. “There is none holy like the LORD”; all holiness is His, and is what He gives by His holy presence. The tabernacle and the temple were not made holy by cleansing, separation or consecration. They became holy when God came in and dwelt there. His taking possession made them holy. In the same way, God makes us holy through His Word, as it brings Christ and the Holy Spirit into us. And the Father cannot do this unless we wait before Him and are still, and give ourselves up to Him in deep dependence and full surrender. It is in prayer offered in the name, the fellowship and the faith of the great Intercessor — “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth” — that the Father’s sanctifying power will be found, and that our knowledge of God’s Word will truly make us holy. How sacred the Morning Watch is! This hour is set apart in a special way for the soul to yield itself up to God’s holiness, to be sanctified through the Word. Let us always remember that the one aim of God’s Word is to make us holy. Let our continual prayer be, “Father, sanctify me in your truth.”

fields.title: Psalm 119 And Its Teaching
fields.body_html:
“Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day.” Psalms 119:97.

In Holy Scripture there is one passage wholly given over to teaching us the place God’s Word ought to have in our esteem, and how we can secure its blessing. It is the longest chapter in the Bible, and in almost every one of its 176 verses the Word is mentioned, under different names. Anyone who really wants to know how to study his Bible according to God’s will ought to make a careful study of this Psalm.

There ought to come a time in his life when he resolves to study its teaching and put it into practice. How can we wonder that our Bible study brings no more spiritual profit and strength, if we neglect the divine guide it offers us for that study? Perhaps you have never once read it through as a whole. If you do not have time, find time — some free Sunday hour, or why not a free week, day or hour? — in which to read it through and try to take in its main thought, or at least to catch its spirit.

If you find this hard to do in one reading, read it more than once. This will make you feel the need to give it more careful thought. The following hints may help you in your study: 1st. Note all the different names by which God’s Word is called.

2nd. Note all the different verbs that express what we ought to feel and do with regard to the Word. Let this lead you to consider carefully the place God’s Word claims in your heart and life, and how every faculty of your being — desire, love, joy, trust, obedience, action — is called out by it.

3rd. Count and note how many times the writer speaks in the past tense of having kept, observed, held fast to and delighted in God’s testimonies. How many times does he say in the present tense that he rejoices in God’s law, loves it and values it? And then how often, in the future tense, does he promise and vow to keep God’s precepts to the end? Put all these together and see how more than a hundred times he presents his soul to God as one who honours and keeps His law. Study this especially as these expressions are linked with his prayers to God, until you have a clear picture of the righteous man whose fervent, effectual prayer avails much.

4th. Then study the prayers themselves, and note the different requests he makes concerning the Word — whether for teaching to understand it and power to keep it, or for the blessing promised in the Word and found in doing it.

Note especially prayers like “Teach me, O LORD, the way of your statutes” and “Give me understanding.” Note also those where the plea is “according to your Word.”

5th. Count the verses that refer to affliction — whether from his own condition, from his enemies, from the sins of the wicked, or from God delaying “to help him” — and learn that it is in times of trouble that we especially need God’s Word, and that only the Word can bring us comfort.

6th. Then comes one of the most important things. Mark how often the little words “you” and “yours” occur, and how often they are understood in every request — “Teach me,” “Quicken me” — and you will see that the whole psalm is a prayer spoken to God. Everything the Psalmist has to say about the Word of God, whether about his own devotion to it or his need for God’s teaching and quickening, is spoken upward, into the face of God. He believes it pleases God, and is good for his own soul, to link his meditation and thoughts on the Word as continually and closely as possible, through prayer, with the living God Himself. Instead of drawing him away from God, every thought about God’s Word leads him into fellowship with God.

For him, the Word of God becomes rich and inexhaustible material for communion with the God whose Word it is, and to whom it is meant to lead. As we gradually gain insight into these truths, we will find new meaning in individual verses.

And when from time to time we take a whole section with its eight verses, we will find how they help lift us up, with and through the Word, into God’s presence and into that life of obedience and joy which says, “I have sworn an oath and confirmed it, to keep your righteous rules.” “Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day.”

Let us seek, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, to have the devotional life this Psalm reveals worked into our Morning Watch. Let God’s Word, every day and before everything else, lead us To God. Let every blessing in it become a matter of prayer — especially our need for divine teaching. Let our deep devotion to it be our childlike plea, and our confidence that the Father will help us. Let our prayers be followed by the vow that, as God quickens and blesses us, we will run in the way of His commandments. And let all that God’s Word brings to us make us all the more eager to carry that Word to others, whether to awaken the life of God in their souls or to strengthen it.

fields.title: The Holy Trinity
fields.body_html:
“For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith—that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.” Ephesians 3: 14-21.

These words have often — and not without good reason — been seen as one of the highest expressions of what a believer’s life on earth can be. And yet this view has its dangers, if it encourages the idea that such an experience is something exceptional and far off, and hides the blessed truth that, though in differing degrees, it is meant to be the certain and present inheritance of every child of God.

Every morning, every believer has as much right as need to say: My Father will strengthen me today with power through His Spirit in the inner self — He is strengthening me even now.

Every day we are to be satisfied with nothing less than Christ dwelling in us by faith, and a life rooted in love and made strong to know the love of Christ. Every day we believe that the blessed work of being filled with all the fullness of God is being prepared, carried forward and completed in us. And every day we ought to be strong in faith in God’s power, giving Him glory in Christ as the One who is able to do more than we ask or think, according to the power of the Spirit at work in us.

Among many other things, these words are remarkable for the way they present the truth of the Holy Trinity as it bears on our practical life. Many Christians understand that at different times in the Christian life it is right and necessary to give special attention to each of the three Persons of the blessed Trinity. But they often find it hard to bring the various truths together into one, and to know how to worship the Three in One.

Our text reveals their wonderful relationship and perfect unity. We have the Spirit within us as the power of God, and yet He does not work at our will, nor at His own. It is the Father who, according to the riches of His glory, grants us to be strengthened “through the Spirit in the inner man.”

It is the Father who does far more abundantly than all we ask or think, “according to the power at work within us.” So far from the Spirit’s presence within us taking the place of God for us, He makes us more absolutely and constantly dependent on the Father. The Spirit can only work as the Father works through Him. We need to hold the two truths together: a deeply reverent, trusting awareness of the Holy Spirit dwelling within us, and a continual, dependent waiting on the Father to work through Him.

It is the same with Christ. We bow our knees to God as Father in the name of the Son. We ask Him to strengthen us through the Spirit for this one purpose: that Christ may dwell in our hearts. So the Son leads to the Father, and the Father in turn reveals the Son in us. And then, as the Son dwells in the heart, and the heart is rooted and grounded in love — drawing its life from divine love as its soil, bearing fruit and doing works of love — we are led on to be filled with all the fullness of God. The whole heart, with the inner and the outer life, becomes the scene of the blessed interplay of the working of the Holy Three. As our hearts believe this, we give glory through Christ to Him who is able, by His Holy Spirit, to do more than we can think.

What a wonderful salvation this is, with our heart as its scene! The Father continually breathing His Spirit into us, and by His daily renewing making the heart fit to be the home of Christ. The Holy Spirit continually revealing Christ and forming Him within us, so that His very nature, disposition and character become ours. The Son imparting His life of love, and leading us on to be filled with all the fullness of God.

This is meant to be our everyday religion. Oh, let us worship the Three-in-One God in the fullness of faith every day! Wherever our Bible study and our prayer lead us, let this always be the centre we go out from and come back to. We were created in the image of the Three-in-One God. The salvation by which God restores us is an inward salvation; it means nothing to us unless it is worked out in our hearts and enjoyed there. The God who saves us can do it in no other way than as the God who dwells within, filling us with all His fullness. Let us worship and wait; let us believe and give Him glory.

Have you ever noticed how often in Ephesians the three Persons of the Trinity are mentioned together?

1. 3. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.

1. 12, 13. So that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory. In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.

1. 17. That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.

2. 18. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

3. 22. In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

4. 4-9. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things.

5. 4-6. There is one body and one Spirit—just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call— one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. 5. Filled with the Spirit, giving thanks to God, in the name of Christ.

6. 10-18. Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. Put on the whole armor of God that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil.

For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the whole armor of God that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace.

In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints. As you study and compare these passages, and try to gather up their teaching into some true and humble idea of the glory of our God, notice especially how intensely practical a truth the Holy Trinity is. Scripture teaches little about its mystery within the divine nature; almost everything it has to say concerns God’s work in us, and our faith in His salvation and our experience of it.

True faith in the Trinity will make us strong, bright, God-possessed Christians: the divine Spirit making Himself one with our life and inner being; the blessed Son dwelling in us as the way to perfect fellowship with God; the Father, through the Spirit and the Son, working out His purpose day by day — that we may be filled with all the fullness of God. Let us bow our knees to the Father! Then the mystery of the Trinity will be known and experienced.

fields.title: In Christ
fields.body_html:
“Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.” John 15: 4.

All teaching moves from the outward to the inward. Once some knowledge of the actual facts has been gained — in words or deeds, in nature or history — the mind is ready to look for the inner meaning hidden in them. It is the same with the teaching of Scripture about Jesus Christ. He is set before us as a man among us, before us and above us, doing work for us here on earth and continuing that work for us still in heaven.

Many Christians never go beyond this — an exalted Lord outside them, whom they trust for what He has done and is doing for them and in them. They know and enjoy very little of the power of the true mystery of Christ in us — of His inward presence as an indwelling Saviour. The first and simpler view is that of the first three Gospels; the second marks the Gospel of St. John. The first is the side of the truth set out in the Scripture doctrine of justification. The second is the teaching about the believer’s union with Christ and his continual abiding, taught especially in St. John and in the letters to the Ephesians and Colossians.

To the Christians for whom this book is written — all of whom ought to be preparing to carry Christ to their fellow men — I cannot say it too earnestly: make sure that this abiding in Christ, and Christ in you, is not only a truth you hold in its right place in your scheme of Gospel doctrine, but that, as a matter of life and experience, it gives life to all your faith in Christ and your fellowship with God. To be in a room means to have everything in it at your disposal — its furniture, its comforts, its lights, its air, its shelter. To be in Christ is to abide in Christ and to know what this means. It is not a matter of intellectual belief or ideas, but a spiritual reality.

Think about who and what Christ is. Consider Him in the five states or stages that mark and reveal His nature and work. He is the Incarnate One, in whom we see how God’s almighty power perfectly united the divine and human natures. Living in Him, we share in the divine nature and in eternal life. He is the Obedient One, living a life of complete surrender to God and perfect dependence on Him. Living in Him, our life becomes one of complete submission to God’s will and continual waiting on His guidance. He is the Crucified One, who died for sin and to sin so that He might take it away. Living in Him, we are free from its curse and its rule, and we live, like Him, in death to the world and to our own will. He is the Risen One, who lives for evermore.

Living in Him, we share His resurrection power and walk in newness of life — a life that has triumphed over sin and death.

He is the Exalted One, sitting on the throne and carrying on His work for the salvation of the world. Living in Him, His love possesses us, and we give ourselves to Him to be used in winning the world back to God. Being in Christ and abiding in Him means nothing less than this: the soul is placed by God Himself in the midst of this wonderful setting of the life of Christ — at once human and divine, wholly given up to God in obedience and sacrifice, wholly filled with God in resurrection life and glory. The nature and character of Jesus Christ — His dispositions and affections, His power and glory — are the element we live in, the air we breathe, the life in which our life exists and grows.

The full revelation of God and His saving love can come in no other way than by indwelling. Because of His divinity and divine power, Christ can dwell in us just so far as we abide in Him. As far as the heart, with its love, is given to Him in faith, and the will in active obedience, He comes in and makes His home in us. We can say, because we know it: Christ lives in me.

And now, to come to our main point: if this life — Christ in us and we in Him — is to be our real, working-day life, its spirit must be renewed and strengthened in the personal fellowship with God with which we begin the day in the Morning Watch.

Our access to God, our sacrifice to God and our expectation from God must all be in Christ, in living fellowship with Him.

Whenever you feel that you want to come nearer to God — to realise more fully His presence or power, His love, will or working; in a word, to have more of God — come to God in Christ. Take before God the very place Christ took on earth on His way to victory and glory. Do it in faith in His indwelling, enabling power in you here on earth. Count confidently on your approach being accepted, not according to what you have attained, but according to the honesty of your heart’s surrender and the completeness of your acceptance in Christ. And you will be led on in the path where Christ living in you and speaking in you will be truth and power.

fields.title: Himself Alone
fields.body_html:
“Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.” John 6: 15.

The Gospels often tell us of Christ going away into solitude to pray. Luke mentions His praying eleven times. Mark tells us in his very first chapter that, after an evening when the whole city had gathered at the door and He had healed many, “And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed.” Before He chose His twelve apostles, “In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God.” This idea of complete withdrawal seems to have made a deep impression on the disciples, and it gave rise to John’s meaningful expression, “Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself,” just as Matthew had also written, “He went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.” Christ felt the need for perfect solitude. Let us humbly try to find out what this means.

1. By Himself alone. Entirely by Himself, alone with Himself. We know how much our dealings with people draw us away from ourselves and drain our strength. The man Christ Jesus knew this too. He felt the need to come back to Himself — to gather all His powers, to renew His awareness of what He was and what He needed, and to realise fully His high destiny, His human weakness and His complete dependence on the Father. How much more does the child of God need this! Whether in the middle of the distractions of worldly business or of religious service, whether for keeping up our own Christian life or for renewing our power to influence people for God, there is always an urgent call to every believer to follow in his Master’s steps, and to find the place and the time where he can truly be by himself alone.

2. By Himself alone, with spiritual realities. It is when we withdraw completely from contact with the things that are seen and temporary that we are free to yield ourselves fully to the powers of the unseen world and let them master us. Jesus needed time and quiet, again and again, to realise the power of the kingdom of darkness He had come to fight and conquer, the need of this great world of mankind He had come to save, and the presence and power of the Father whose will He had come to do. Nothing is more essential in Christian service than that a person should at times set himself to think intensely about the spiritual realities that are so familiar to him as a matter of knowledge, and yet often have so little power over his heart and life.

The truths of eternity have infinite power; they are often so powerless because we do not give them time to reveal themselves. By himself alone — this is the only cure.

3. By Himself alone, with God the Father. It is sometimes said that work is worship and that service is fellowship. If ever there was a man who could do without special times of solitude and fellowship, it was our blessed Lord. But He could not do His work, or keep up His fellowship in full power, without His quiet time. As a man, He felt the need to bring all His work, past and future, and lay it before the Father, and to renew His sense of absolute dependence on the Father’s love in times of special fellowship. When He said, “the Son can do nothing of Himself” and “as I hear so I speak,” He was simply expressing the plain truth of His relationship to God; and it was this that made His going apart both a necessity and an inexpressible joy. If only every servant of God understood and practised this blessed art! If only the Church knew how to train its children in some sense of this high and holy privilege — that every believer may, and must, have his time when he is truly by himself alone with God! Oh, the thought of having God all alone to myself, and of knowing that God has me all alone to Himself!

4. By Himself alone, with the Word. As a man, our Lord had to learn God’s Word as a child; through the long years of His life in Nazareth He fed on that Word and made it His own. In His solitude He talked with the Father about all that the Word said of Him, and about all the will of God it revealed for Him to do. One of the deepest lessons the Christian has to learn is that the Word without the living God does little good; that the blessing of the Word comes when it brings us to the living God; and that the Word we receive from the mouth of God brings with it the power to know it and to do it.

Let us learn the lesson: only personal fellowship with God in secret can make the Word life and power.

5. By Himself alone, in prayer. What an inexpressible privilege prayer is, allowing a person to lay his whole life open before God and to ask for His teaching and His strength! Just try for a moment to imagine what prayer meant to Jesus — what adoring worship, what humble love, what childlike pleading for everything He needed. We can no more grasp this rightly than we can realise what blessedness awaits the person who knows how to follow in Christ’s steps, and to prove the very utmost God can do for one who makes this his chief joy — to be with Him, by himself alone.

By Himself alone. How deeply these words open up to us the secret of Christ’s life on earth, and of the life He now lives in us by His Holy Spirit! This is one of the most blessed parts of that life: He reveals and imparts to us all that the words mean — by Himself alone.

fields.title: Soul-winning
fields.body_html:
“The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise.” Proverbs 11: 30.

In an article on “A Spiritual Awakening” by H. W. Oldham, in The Student Movement for February 1901, I found the following sentences: “In the constitutions of most Student Christian Unions it is stated that the chief aim of the Union is to lead students to become disciples of Jesus Christ. But if the question is pressed home — ‘Are students actually being won from indifference and unbelief to faith in Jesus Christ?’ — the answer must be that, although this is the case in a few instances, in most Unions it is very doubtful. Some Unions, discouraged by past failure, have become sceptical about the possibility of winning men for Christ in circumstances as difficult as their own. They may to some extent carry on the traditional methods of outreach, but they have stopped expecting to do more than strengthen those who already have faith.

The Executive of the General College Department has deliberately put the spiritual awakening of students at the forefront of its policy. If the local Unions will rally round the Executive, we may fully expect to see God at work in the lives of those around us.

‘The love that won us can win many.’ It is right to recognise how serious it is to adopt this aim. It involves close companionship with Jesus Christ in holy living, in self-sacrifice and in loving service; it requires submission to the correction and control of God’s Spirit…. We must lift the aim of winning students for Christ out of the background of our work and put it first. Our Unions have more than enough mechanical workers. They need men and women with definite aims, who will think and pray, and pray and work, until their Union is a fit instrument in God’s hand for transforming the lives of students.”

In an editorial in the same issue, we read about the Day of Prayer: “There are many confessions and many requests we will have to make on the Day of Prayer; but for our part, we feel that the most urgent must be a prayer for a spiritual awakening. We have gradually been recognising that most of our Unions are not winning men for Christ, and some have begun to realise with dismay that this fact has caused them very little sorrow. ‘It is certainly a misfortune that students have not been won, but — what can we do?’ Truly a spiritual awakening is needed — needed in our own hearts. When it comes, we will soon find out what to do. Where is the passionate longing to help people? Where is the urgent prayer for our brother that will not take no for an answer?

At the very heart of the whole matter is our lack of interest. Only what interests us will influence others.

Only when, deep down among the eternal concerns of our soul, there burns a passionate desire to lead people to Christ will we meet those who need our help and will welcome it. Only words and deeds that burst out of a burning passion to help people find opportunities to influence lives. For it is only where there is a desire like this — since without Him we are powerless either to find those who are in need or, having found them, to help them. Shall we not ask together that a passion for souls may be born in each of us on the Day of Prayer?”

To this let me add an extract from an article on “Indian Needs” in the January issue of the same paper. The writer (Rev. W. E. S. Holland, formerly Travelling Secretary of the B.C.C.U.) had spoken of the central purpose in founding mission colleges as being “the personal influence which the teachers” — and of four of the largest Indian mission colleges, “that their time is so fully taken up with lecturing that they have neither time nor spirit for personal contact with their students. Five or six hours a day, with several more in preparation, in an Indian climate, leave a man exhausted, with neither time nor nervous energy for that most intense of all work, dealing individually with a man about his soul.”

He ends his paper with these words: “40,000 men are wanted — no fewer — if all India is to hear. And yet one almost shrinks from making an appeal for men. Why? For fear that men should come who would only take up room. For missionary work is, after all, simply soul-winning. And there is nothing to make a man a soul-winner in India who has not been one at home.

A sense of duty, or of the great need, may bring a man to India. Nothing can enable him to live a missionary life out here, year after year, except a burning love for Christ that compels him to sacrifice, and a life of soul-winning at home.”

What thoughts these extracts suggest about the work of soul-winning! That it is the first great requirement in a missionary. That going to a mission field will not necessarily make anyone a soul-winner. That it is at home, before one enters the mission field, that the spirit of self-sacrifice and soul-winning must be gained and put into practice. That training its members in the art of soul-winning is one of the chief aims of the Student Movement, and practising it will be the measure of the movement’s strength and success. That the danger is always there of our slipping out of this into traditional, mechanical methods. And that continual, fervent prayer — united and private — ought to be made for more love for souls, and continual, earnest effort — united and private — put forth in every Students’ Union, so that our companions may be won for Christ.

The great characteristic of the divine life, whether in God, in Christ or in us, is love seeking to save the lost. Let this be the Christian life we cultivate: a love that finds its blessedness in saving people. This life can be cultivated in no other way than by close personal attachment to Jesus and daily fellowship with Him as a Friend we love.

It is in the inner chamber that this fellowship with the Father and the Son is to be kept up. It is here that the Father who sees us in secret will reward us openly.

fields.title: The Power of Intercession
fields.body_html:
“So Delilah said to Samson, ‘Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you.’” Judges 16:6.

This is the question we would love to have answered by the men who, in ancient and in later times, have had power with God as intercessors for others, and have prevailed. More than one person who has wanted to give himself to this ministry has been surprised at how hard he has found it to rejoice in it, to persevere and to prevail. Let us study the lives of the leaders and heroes of the world of prayer; perhaps we will discover some of the elements of their success.

A true intercessor is a man who knows that God knows him, and that his heart and life are wholly given up to God and His glory. This is the only condition on which an officer at the court of an earthly king could expect to have much influence. Moses, Elijah, Daniel and Paul prove that it is the same in the spiritual world. Our blessed Lord Himself is the proof of it. He did not save us by intercession but by self-sacrifice. His power of intercession is rooted in His sacrifice: it claims and receives what the sacrifice won. We have this put so clearly in the last words of Isaiah 53: “He poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors, yet he bore the sin of many, and” — study this in connection with the whole chapter, of which it is the crown — “and makes intercession for the transgressors.” He first gave Himself up to the will of God.

There He won the power to influence and guide that will. He gave Himself for sinners in all-consuming love, and so He won the power to intercede for them. There is no other path for us. It is the person who seeks to enter personally into death with Christ, and who gives himself wholly for God and for others, who will dare to be bold like Moses or Elijah and will persevere like Daniel or Paul. Wholehearted devotion and obedience to God are the first marks of an intercessor.

You complain that you do not feel able to pray, and you ask how you can be made fit for it. You speak a great deal about the weakness of your faith in God, your love for souls and your delight in prayer. Anyone who is to have power in intercession must stop these complaints. He must know that he has a nature perfectly suited to the work. An apple tree is expected to bear apples only because it has the apple nature within it.

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.” The eye was created to see — how beautifully fitted it is for its work! You were created in Christ to pray.

It is your very nature as a child of God. The Spirit has been sent into your heart — to do what? To cry, Abba, Father; to draw your heart upward in childlike prayer. The Holy Spirit prays in us with groanings that cannot be uttered, with a divine power that our minds and feelings cannot understand. If you want to be an intercessor, learn to give the Holy Spirit far more honour than is usually given Him. Believe that He is praying within you, and then be strong and of good courage. As you pray, be still before God, to believe in this wonderful power of prayer within you and to yield to it.

But is there not so much conscious sinfulness and failure in our prayer? True — but have you not learned what it is to pray in the name of Christ?

Does the name not mean living power? Do you not know that you are in Christ and He in you? That your whole life is hidden in His and bound up with it, and His whole life is hidden and at work in you? Whoever is to intercede with power must be very clear that Christ and he are one in the work of intercession — not only in thought and reckoning, but in the most actual, living, divine reality. He appears before God clothed with the name and the nature, the righteousness and worthiness, the image, spirit and life of Christ. Do not spend most of your prayer time repeating your request, but humbly, quietly and confidently claim your place in Christ, your perfect union with Him and your access to God in Him. It is the person who comes to God in Christ — bringing to the Father that Christ in whom He delights, as his life, his law and his only trust — who will have the power to intercede.

Intercession is above all a work of faith. Not the faith that only tries to believe that the prayer will be heard, but the faith that is at home among heavenly realities. A faith that does not worry about its own nothingness and weakness, because it is living in Christ. A faith that does not make its hope depend on its feelings, but on the faithfulness of the Three-in-One God, in what each Person has undertaken to do in prayer. A faith that has overcome the world, and sacrifices the visible in order to be wholly free for the spiritual, the heavenly and the eternal, and to take possession of them. A faith that knows it is heard and receives what it asks, and so quietly and deliberately keeps on with its request until the answer comes. The true intercessor must be a person of faith.

The intercessor must be a messenger — someone who holds himself ready and earnestly offers himself to receive the answer personally and to hand it on. Praying and working go together. We see the same in Elijah: the urgency of his prayer in secret is matched by his zeal for God in public, as he saw the sin of the nation.

It is a greater thing, as an intercessor, to receive that blessing personally, and to go out from God’s presence knowing that we have secured something we can pass on. fields.title: The Intercessor
fields.body_html:
“Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working. Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth.” James 5: 16, 17.

Nothing weakens the force of the call to imitate the example of the saints of Scripture as much as the idea that theirs are exceptional cases, and that what we see in them is not to be expected of everyone. God’s aim in Scripture is the very opposite. He gives us these men for our instruction and encouragement, as samples of what His grace can do — living embodiments of what His will and our nature both demand and make possible.

It was precisely to meet this very common error, and to give confidence to all of us who aim at a life of effective prayer, that James wrote: “Elijah was a man with a nature like ours.” Since there was no difference between his nature and ours, or between the grace that worked in him and the grace that works in us, there is no reason why we should not pray effectively as he did. If our prayer is to have power, we must seek to have something of Elijah’s spirit.

The longing — let me seek grace to pray like Elijah — is perfectly right, and very necessary. If we honestly seek the secret of his power in prayer, the path he walked will open up to us. We will find it in his life with God, his work for God and his trust in God.

Elijah lived with God. Prayer is the voice of our life. As a man lives, so he prays. It is not the words or thoughts that fill his set times of prayer, but the bent of his heart, seen in his desires and actions, that God regards as his real prayer. Life speaks louder and truer than the lips. To pray well, I must live well. Whoever seeks to live with God will learn to know His mind and to please Him, so that he will be able to pray according to His will. Think how Elijah, in his first message to Ahab, spoke of “As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand.” Think of his solitude at the brook Cherith, receiving his bread from God through the ravens, and then at Zarephath through the help of a poor widow. He walked with God and learned to know God well; when the time came, he knew how to pray to a God he had tested and proved. Only out of a life of true fellowship with God can the prayer of faith be born. Let the link between life and prayer be clear and close. As we give ourselves to walking with God, we will learn to pray.

Elijah worked for God. He went where God sent him. He did what God commanded him. He stood up for God and His service. He bore witness against the people and their sins. All who heard him could say: “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth.” His prayers were all connected with his work for God. He was as much a man of action as a man of prayer. When he prayed down first the drought and then the rain, it was as part of his prophetic work, so that the people might be brought back to God by judgment and by mercy.

When Elijah prayed down fire from heaven on the sacrifice, it was so that God might be known as the true God. All he asked was for the glory of God. How often believers seek power in prayer so that they can obtain good gifts for themselves! That hidden selfishness robs them of the power and of the answer. It is when self is lost in the desire for God’s glory, and our life is devoted to working for God, that the power to pray can come.

God lives to love, save and bless people. The believer who gives himself up to God’s service in this will find in it new life in prayer. Work for others proves that our prayer for them is genuine. Work for God shows both our need and our right to pray boldly. Cultivate the awareness that you are wholly given up to His service, and say it out loud before God; it will strengthen your confidence that He hears you.

Elijah trusted in God. He had learned to trust Him for his personal needs in times of famine, and he dared to trust Him for greater things in answer to prayer for His people. What confidence in God’s hearing him we see in his appeal to the God who answers by fire! What confidence that God would do what he asked, when he announced to Ahab the abundance of rain that was coming, and then, with his face to the ground, pleaded for it, while his servant came back six times with the message, “There is nothing.” Unwavering confidence in God’s promise and character — together with personal fellowship with God, proved in work for God — gave power to the effectual prayer of the righteous man.

The inner chamber is the place where this has to be learned. The Morning Watch is the training school where we are to exercise the grace that can make us fit to pray like Elijah. Let us not be afraid. The God of Elijah still lives; the Spirit who was in him lives in us. Let us give up the narrow and selfish views of prayer that aim only at enough grace to keep us standing.

Let us cultivate the awareness Elijah had of living wholly for God, and we will learn to pray like him. Prayer will bring to ourselves and to others the new and blessed experience that our prayers too are effectual and avail much. In the power of that redeeming Intercessor, who ever lives to pray, let us take courage and not be afraid. We have given ourselves to God; we are working for Him. We are learning to know Him and trust Him.

We are learning to know Him. We can count on the life of God in us — the Holy Spirit living in us — to lead us on into this grace too: the effectual prayer of the righteous man that avails much.

THE END
